student.headline: Clean, separate, cook and chill—while preventing cuts, burns, slips and allergic reactions.
hazards: Knives, graters and broken items can cause cuts.
Hot surfaces, steam, boiling liquids and oil can cause serious burns.
Raw food, dirty hands and shared equipment can spread harmful germs or allergens.
Spills, wet floors, clutter and damaged electrical equipment can cause injury.
beforeStart: Tell the teacher about allergies, illness, cuts or anything that could affect food safety.
Wash and dry your hands properly; tie back hair, secure sleeves and put on a clean apron.
Check that your bench, utensils and equipment are clean, complete and safe.
Read the method, identify hot/sharp steps, and separate raw food from ready-to-eat food.
dos: Wash hands after touching raw food, rubbish, your face or anything dirty.
Use the correct knife and board; cut on a stable surface and carry knives safely.
Turn pan handles inward, use dry oven gloves, and lift lids away from your face.
Clean spills immediately, cook food as instructed, and chill or store it promptly.
donts: Do not eat, taste or share food until the teacher says it is safe.
Do not use the same unwashed board, knife or utensil for raw and ready-to-eat food.
Do not leave knives in sinks, carry hot pans across a crowded room or put water on burning oil.
Do not use damaged electrical equipment or touch switches with wet hands.
stop: There is a cut, burn, allergic reaction, illness or suspected contamination.
Oil, a pan, appliance or cloth begins to smoke or catch fire.
A knife, plug, lead, appliance, oven glove or piece of equipment is damaged.
Food temperatures, storage, labels or ingredients are uncertain, or anything feels unsafe.
student.note: General kitchen rules apply alongside the recipe, allergy controls and exact equipment SOP. They do not replace teacher instruction, permission or supervision.

teacher.overview: General personal hygiene, food-safety, housekeeping and injury-prevention controls for student work in a school food-technology kitchen. This record supports, but does not replace, recipe-specific risk assessment, allergen management, equipment SOPs, the school emergency plan or applicable food-control requirements.
hazards: Cuts and punctures from knives, graters, broken glass, sharp tins and powered food-preparation equipment.
Burns and scalds from ovens, hobs, hot surfaces, steam, boiling liquids and hot oil.
Foodborne illness from poor hand hygiene, cross-contamination, inadequate cooking, unsafe cooling or unsuitable storage.
Allergic reaction caused by unidentified ingredients, cross-contact or incorrect serving.
Slips, trips, electric shock and fire arising from spills, clutter, wet hands, damaged equipment or poor supervision.
riskAssessment: The recipe, ingredients, allergens, equipment, student competence and room layout change the risk and must be checked for every lesson.
Good personal hygiene and separation of raw and ready-to-eat foods are essential controls but do not replace validated cooking, cooling and storage instructions.
Students require close supervision for sharp, hot, powered or allergen-sensitive processes until competency is demonstrated.
preStart: Check medical/allergy information, recipe ingredients, substitutions and cross-contact controls before food is issued.
Confirm handwashing facilities, cleaning materials, first aid, fire controls, refrigeration and required equipment are available and serviceable.
Set safe movement routes and work zones, allocate equipment, and remove damaged items from service.
Brief students on the recipe's critical hygiene, cooking, cooling, storage and emergency steps.
safeUse: Require effective handwashing and clean protective clothing; exclude or manage students with symptoms, uncovered wounds or contamination risks according to local procedure.
Separate raw animal products from cooked and ready-to-eat food, including hands, boards, utensils, cloths and storage.
Teach and supervise safe knife, hot-liquid, oven, hob and powered-appliance techniques.
Use the recipe/local food-safety plan for required cooking, holding, cooling and refrigeration controls.
Maintain prompt spill control, waste removal, surface cleaning and uncluttered movement routes.
Prevent allergen cross-contact and verify ingredients before food is tasted, shared or served.
shutdown: Switch off, unplug or isolate appliances as required and allow hot equipment to cool safely.
Store or dispose of food promptly using local time/temperature and labelling rules.
Wash, sanitise where required, dry and store equipment; remove waste and leave floors and benches clean and dry.
Report injuries, allergic reactions, contamination, equipment faults and temperature-control failures.
restrictions: Students must not taste, share or serve food until the teacher confirms that hygiene, cooking, allergen and storage requirements have been met.
Deep frying, high-risk powered equipment and other restricted processes require their own approved SOP and supervision.
Recipe-specific, allergy-specific and local food-control requirements take priority over this general record.
disposal: Dispose of food, broken glass, sharps, hot oil, chemicals and general waste using separate approved local procedures; never pour hot oil into a sink.
storage: Cover, label and store food at the required temperature; keep raw animal products separated and below ready-to-eat food. Store knives, chemicals and appliances securely.
furtherInformation: Use the current PHS allergy information, recipe plan, equipment SOPs and any applicable food-control documentation.
firstAid: Stop the activity, make the area safe, alert the teacher and follow the PHS emergency/first-aid procedure for cuts, burns, electric shock, fire or illness.
Treat suspected anaphylaxis as an emergency and follow the student's individual health plan and school emergency procedure.
teacherChecks: Adapt this record to the exact recipe, ingredients, allergens, equipment, room and student group.
Check current New Zealand Food Safety guidance and PHS procedures before approval.
Confirm students understand handwashing, raw/cooked separation, allergen controls and when to stop and report.
Do not treat this draft as automatic permission for student use.

student.headline: Cool cooked food quickly and safely. Use only the food and settings your teacher gives you.
hazards: Very cold food or surfaces can injure skin
Damaged electrical equipment can shock
Poor cooling can let harmful germs multiply
beforeStart: Get teacher permission and follow the machine instructions.
Wash your hands and use clean containers.
Check the food is suitable for blast chilling.
Use protective gloves when handling very cold items.
dos: Place food in the chiller as your teacher shows you.
Keep containers clean, covered and clearly identified.
Close the door properly and use the correct programme.
Move chilled food to the correct storage as soon as instructed.
donts: Do not put unsuitable items into the chiller.
Do not use a damaged machine, plug or lead.
Do not handle very cold items with bare hands if gloves are required.
Do not change settings unless your teacher tells you to.
stop: The machine is damaged or not cooling properly.
Food has been left warm for too long.
You get a cold burn or numb skin.
Something looks, smells or feels unsafe.

teacher.overview: Use of commercial blast chillers to reduce the temperature of food quickly.
teacher.supervision: Set locally from the source restrictions, student maturity, class size and Pukekohe High School procedure.
teacher.training: Confirm competency and local authorisation before use.
hazards: Electric shock: Any electrically powered item presents a shock risk if it is damaged.
Food poisoning (Infection): Gastrointestinal infection results from eating, or hand to mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxic products.
riskAssessment: Electric shock: With all electrical equipment there is a risk of electric shock. However blast chillers should be installed by a qualified electrician / plumber and have an appropriately fused switch-disconnect or if hard wired an isolating plug. If the appliance’s rating requires one it should also have a ventilation extraction system. Correct installation and regular maintenance checks reduce the shock risk to minimal.

Food poisoning (Infection): Harmful bacteria require food, moisture, warmth and time to survive and multiply. All reproduce rapidly at temperatures around 37 °C (ie, body temperature) but many can multiply at lower or higher temperatures. By blast chilling the risk of bacterial reproduction is considerably reduced.
preStart: The blast chiller should be included in a regular planned maintenance programme and also be part of regular visual checks by a competent person at suitable frequencies to identify any faults that require maintenance to reduce the risk of incorrect operation.
Manufacturers instructions should be followed at all times.
Only suitable ingredients or foods should be put into the blast chiller.
Protective gloves should be worn when removing cold items from the chiller.
safeUse: The blast chiller should be included in a regular planned maintenance programme and also be part of regular visual checks by a competent person at suitable frequencies to identify any faults that require maintenance to reduce the risk of incorrect operation.
Manufacturers instructions should be followed at all times.
Only suitable ingredients or foods should be put into the blast chiller.
Protective gloves should be worn when removing cold items from the chiller.
disposal: For disposal see 3.034.
furtherInformation: Blast chillers should be included in a regular planned maintenance programme and also be part of regular visual checks by a competent person at suitable frequencies to identify any faults that require maintenance to reduce the risk of incorrect operation.
firstAid: Freezer burns to the skin: Run affected area under tepid running water for 10 minutes. Cover with a dry dressing. If severe seek further medical advice.

student.headline: Food tests use chemicals. Wear eye protection, use only the test your teacher gives you and keep flames away from ethanol.
hazards: Some test chemicals can irritate or burn skin and eyes
Some reagents are harmful or toxic
Ethanol used for fat tests is highly flammable
Hot water baths and hot test tubes can burn
beforeStart: Put on safety glasses before handling test chemicals.
Do the test only in the room and setup your teacher has approved.
Use only teacher-prepared reagents and the approved test method.
Check which tests are allowed for your year level.
Make sure there are no flames or pilot lights when ethanol is used.
dos: Use small amounts and keep test tubes in a rack.
Heat test tubes only by the method your teacher shows you.
Keep reagent droppers and containers separate.
Wash hands and clean the work area after testing.
donts: Do not taste any test chemical or tested food.
Do not use Millon’s reagent unless your teacher confirms you are allowed.
Do not use Fehling’s solution or Clinitest unless your teacher confirms you are allowed.
Do not use ethanol near a flame.
stop: A chemical splashes into eyes or onto skin.
A container is unlabelled, damaged or leaking.
You smell strong fumes or see a spill.
You are unsure which reagent or test to use.

teacher.overview: Tests to identify the presence of sugars, starch, proteins, fats and vitamin C.
teacher.supervision: Set locally from the source restrictions, student maturity, class size and Pukekohe High School procedure.
teacher.training: Confirm competency and local authorisation before use.
hazards: Corrosive: Solutions of sodium hydroxide at sufficient strength and Millon’s reagent are corrosive.
Toxic: Millon’s reagent contains toxic components.
Harmful: The precipitate in Benedict’s test and solid iodine are harmful.
Irritant: The CLEAPSS modification of the Biuret test uses an irritant solution.
Highly Flammable: The test for fats uses highly flammable ethanol (methylated spirit).
riskAssessment: Corrosive: Tests using corrosive solutions can be avoided.
Toxic: Tests using toxic solutions can be avoided.
Harmful: The main risk here is to the person preparing the iodine solution with a minor risk when washing up after the Benedict’s test.
Irritant: There is a risk to the eyes when using these irritant solutions.
Highly Flammable: Ethanol always presents a risk of fire.
preStart: Food chemical testing is best done in a properly equipped Science laboratory with specialist science technician help.
The corrosive and toxic risks can be avoided by using alternatives.
Solutions should be prepared by a trained technician wearing gloves and eye protection.
Those using irritant solutions should wear eye protection.
safeUse: Food chemical testing is best done in a properly equipped Science laboratory with specialist science technician help.
The corrosive and toxic risks can be avoided by using alternatives.
Solutions should be prepared by a trained technician wearing gloves and eye protection.
Those using irritant solutions should wear eye protection.
Whenever ethanol is used, all naked flames and pilot lights in the vicinity should be extinguished.
restrictions: Millon’s reagent should not be used by pupils or students below year 12.
Fehling’s solutions and Clinitest tablets should not be used by those below year 9 (see over).
All the other tests are suitable for use by responsible pupils of year 7 & above.
disposal: Small quantities of reagents after tests may be diluted with lots of water and flushed into the foul-water drain. (See PS 31, Disposal of Waste in Design & Technology.)
storage: All of these test reagents should be stored in a secure place, away from food. If more than 500 ml of ethanol is kept, it should be in a cabinet designed for highly flammable liquids.

student.headline: Clean as you go. Use only the cleaner your teacher gives you, protect your skin and eyes when required, and never mix cleaners.
hazards: Wet floors can cause slips
Cleaning products can irritate skin or eyes
Sprays can be breathed in or get into eyes
Mixing cleaning products can make dangerous gases
beforeStart: Clear food away before using cleaning products.
Read the label and teacher instructions.
Wear gloves or eye protection if the product requires them.
Keep sprays away from flames and hot equipment.
dos: Clean spills promptly.
Wash food-contact surfaces with the correct product and method.
Rinse surfaces when the product requires it.
Dry surfaces with a clean cloth or paper towel.
donts: Never mix cleaning products.
Do not spray cleaners near faces, food or flames.
Do not use a product you have not been given permission to use.
Do not leave wet floors or benches without warning others.
stop: A cleaner splashes into eyes or onto skin.
You smell strong fumes.
A product is unlabelled or you do not know what it is.

teacher.overview: General cleaning activities.
teacher.supervision: Set locally from the source restrictions, student maturity, class size and Pukekohe High School procedure.
teacher.training: Confirm competency and local authorisation before use.
hazards: Allergic reaction: Some agents contain substances that produce allergic reactions.
Toxic or harmful: Some agents contain substances that are toxic or harmful.
Corrosive: Some agents contain substances that are corrosive.
Irritant: Some agents contain substances that are irritant.
Flammable: Some agents contain substances that are flammable or highly flammable.
or highly flammable
riskAssessment: Allergic reaction: Many people are aware of allergic reactions to some substances or groups of substances. Some people have become ‘sensitised’, ie, even a very small dose of the allergen then produces the reaction. Substances likely to cause sensitisation are identified by risk phrases R42 & 43.
Toxic or harmful: Agents presenting these risks are identified by hazard warnings that may vary with different formulations of the same substance.
Corrosive: Agents presenting these risks are identified by hazard warnings.
Irritant: Agents presenting these risks are identified by hazard warnings.
Flammable: Cleaners may contain flammable components but a greater risk is presented by
or highly flammable: preparations applied as aerosols: the propellant is often highly flammable.
preStart: Training in the safe use of cleaning agents is required by all staff likely to use them.
Simple allergic reactions (dermatitis) can be prevented by the use of gloves or by avoiding the agent.
Once sensitisation has occurred, it is difficult to avoid the reaction other than by a change of job.
It is essential to read the label on the container to ascertain the level of risk and the precautions required to control it.
safeUse: Training in the safe use of cleaning agents is required by all staff likely to use them.
Simple allergic reactions (dermatitis) can be prevented by the use of gloves or by avoiding the agent.
Once sensitisation has occurred, it is difficult to avoid the reaction other than by a change of job.
It is essential to read the label on the container to ascertain the level of risk and the precautions required to control it.
Gloves and eye protection must be worn when using any agent with ‘corrosive’ on the label.
An irritant agent should be handled with gloves.
If possible, the use of cleaning agents in aerosol spray cans should be avoided but, if used, all naked flames should be extinguished.
Care should be taken to see that the contents are not sprayed into the eyes or where they will be inhaled.
restrictions: The separate sheets describe restrictions in the use of certain cleaning agents, where relevant.

Because of the possibility of misuse and materials being sprayed into eyes or flames, it would probably be advisable to restrict the use of pressurised, aerosol cans and other sprays to responsible pupils in year 11 and above.
disposal: Unwanted cleaning liquids may be diluted and flushed away down the foul-water drain so long as the acidity / alkalinity is adjusted to a pH between 5.5 and 9. Empty containers should be rinsed out before placing them in the refuse. Empty aerosol cans should not be incinerated as the residual propellant may explode.
storage: All cleaning agents containing hazardous substances must be stored adequately, away from food areas, so that they cannot be misused. The cupboard should be locked and labelled. Aerosol cans must be stored away from sources of heat (ie, below 50 °C).
furtherInformation: It is necessary to wash all work surfaces thoroughly and regularly, on every day that practical work with food is done, using hot water and detergent.
The inside of the refrigerator and shelves of food storage cupboards should also be washed before drips or spills accumulate, at least once each week.
After washing, the surfaces should be dried with a clean, dry cloth or disposable paper towel.
Wet surfaces are a potential breeding ground for bacteria.
See individual sheets 3.004 to 3.009.
Co-operation with cleaning staff over the methods to be used in food technology areas is essential.
firstAid: Cleaning agents are: Obtain medical attention. Irrigate immediately with water, holding eyelids apart and
sprayed into the eyes: continue until the patient reaches hospital.

Allergic reaction: If patients show anxiety, red, blotchy skin, swelling of the face and neck and puffiness around the eyes, they could be suffering from a serious allergic reaction. Call an ambulance and prop such a patient in a sitting position in case breathing problems develop.
Anaphylactic shock: If patients suffer from impaired breathing and also has a rapid pulse, they may be

(major allergic reaction): going into anaphylactic shock. Check to see if the patients are carrying an Epi-Pen or syringe of adrenaline; if so help them to administer it. Call an ambulance and prop such a patient in a sitting position.

student.headline: Bleach can hurt skin and eyes and can make toxic gas if mixed. Use only the diluted product your teacher gives you.
hazards: Bleach can irritate or burn skin and eyes
Bleach can be harmful if swallowed
Bleach mixed with acids can release toxic chlorine gas
beforeStart: Get teacher permission before using bleach.
Check the product and dilution your teacher gives you.
Wear gloves and eye protection when instructed.
Keep all other cleaning products away.
dos: Use only the amount needed.
Keep bleach away from food until cleaning is finished.
Rinse food-contact items thoroughly when required.
Wash hands after cleaning.
donts: Never mix bleach with descaler, acids or any other cleaner.
Do not use corrosive bleach below Year 12.
Do not splash, spray or play with cleaning products.
Do not take bleach from the storage area without permission.
stop: Bleach gets into eyes, mouth or onto skin.
You smell a strong chlorine-like gas.
The product is stronger than expected or unlabelled.
Someone feels short of breath or unwell.

teacher.overview: Cleaning operations to remove stains using liquids, powders or tablet cleaners.
teacher.supervision: Set locally from the source restrictions, student maturity, class size and Pukekohe High School procedure.
teacher.training: Confirm competency and local authorisation before use.
hazards: Corrosive: Bleaching solutions containing sodium hypochlorite [sodium chlorate(I)] with more than 10% active chlorine and bleaching powder containing calcium hypochlorite [calcium chlorate(I)] are rated corrosive.

Irritant: Bleaching solutions containing sodium hypochlorite (with between 5 and 10% active chlorine) or hydrogen peroxide and bleach tablets containing sodium dichloroisocyanurate are rated irritant. Powders containing sodium perborate are also irritant.
riskAssessment: Corrosive: Solutions classified as corrosive are very hazardous, causing severe damage to the eyes and burns to the skin or alimentary canal, if swallowed. Most ‘concentrated’ bleach solutions available commercially are, however, not so strong as this. Calcium hypochlorite is very dangerous to the skin and eyes. It readily raises dust that could be inhaled or damage the eyes.

Irritant: Bleaches employing hydrogen peroxide as the active ingredient will not usually be sufficiently concentrated to present a major risk in normal use but should be treated as irritant. ‘Bleach’ powders containing sodium perborate will be irritant to the eyes.
preStart: Bleaches that are corrosive require the user to wear a face shield and gloves when dispensing a liquid.
Gloves are sufficient when using a scouring powder1.
Bleaches that are labelled irritant require the eyes to be protected with safety spectacles and gloves should be worn to protect the skin.
Marigold Suregrip GO4Y or Blue Nitrile G25B are recommended.
safeUse: Bleaches that are corrosive require the user to wear a face shield and gloves when dispensing a liquid.
Gloves are sufficient when using a scouring powder1.
Bleaches that are labelled irritant require the eyes to be protected with safety spectacles and gloves should be worn to protect the skin.
Marigold Suregrip GO4Y or Blue Nitrile G25B are recommended.
See CLEAPSS publication PS 50, Gloves as personal Protective Equipment for a full discussion.
restrictions: Pupils below year 12 should not be permitted to use bleach solutions or powders that are corrosive, though they may use diluted solutions under supervision.
Do not mix bleach with other cleaning agents
disposal: Small quantities of bleaches can be mixed with a bucket-full of water and flushed down the foul-water drain. Solids and empty containers can be added to other solid waste.
storage: All bleaches should be stored away from food areas and in a safe and secure place so that they cannot be taken by pupils without permission and misused. As hypochlorite and hydrogen peroxide bleaches deteriorate over time, it is safest to discard any stock that is more than 2 years old.
furtherInformation: It is, of course, essential to rinse containers thoroughly after cleaning them with bleaches.
Bleaching powder, calcium hypochlorite, is an oxidising agent; cloths used with the powder might later ignite.
Always rinse out such cloths thoroughly to remove traces of the powder.
If bleach containing sodium hypochlorite is mixed with acids, the toxic gas chlorine will be released.
Cleaning agents such as descalers and some lavatory cleaners contain acid but it may not always be possible to determine if other cleaners have acidic contents.
Therefore, under no circumstances must bleach be mixed with, or used at the same time as, any other cleaning agent.
Co-operation with cleaning staff over the methods to be used in food technology areas is essential.

Chlorine is liberated: Remove individual to fresh air and seek medical attention.

clothes: of water. If a large area is affected or blistering occurs, seek medical attention. Soak contaminated clothing and rinse repeatedly.

teacher.overview: The removal of scale from hard water from sinks, taps, toilet bowls, washbasins, baths, kettles and steam irons. All use some form of acid as the active ingredient.
teacher.supervision: Set locally from the source restrictions, student maturity, class size and Pukekohe High School procedure.
teacher.training: Confirm competency and local authorisation before use.
hazards: Corrosive: The acid component may be sodium hydrogensulfate or citric, formic, hydrochloric, phosphoric or sulfamic (aminosulfonic) acid. Those containing more than 10% formic acid, 25% hydrochloric acid, 25% phosphoric acid or 18% sodium hydrogensulfate are corrosive.
Irritant: Descalers containing between 2 to 10% formic acid, 10 to 25% hydrochloric acid, 10 to 25% phosphoric acid, 6 to 18% sodium hydrogensulfate or sulfamic acid are irritant.
riskAssessment: Corrosive: The concentration of acid used varies considerably so that the level of risk in using different products is similarly variable. The ‘heavy duty’ formulations, classified as corrosive, are very hazardous, causing severe damage to the eyes and burns to the skin or alimentary canal, if swallowed.

Irritant: The majority of descalers are more dilute but still irritant to the eyes or skin. At even lower concentrations of acid or if citric acid is the active ingredient, there may be no hazard warning on the product label but sensitive skin could be affected and eye contact gives discomfort.
preStart: It is essential to wear gloves when using corrosive products.
It is very strongly advised that the user wears a face shield when dispensing corrosive liquids and that these strong ones are avoided if this protection is not available.
When using products which are powders, ensure that no dust is raised which could be inhaled or get into the eyes.
When using irritant descalers, it is recommended that gloves are worn and that the eyes should be protected with safety spectacles.
safeUse: It is essential to wear gloves when using corrosive products.
It is very strongly advised that the user wears a face shield when dispensing corrosive liquids and that these strong ones are avoided if this protection is not available.
When using products which are powders, ensure that no dust is raised which could be inhaled or get into the eyes.
When using irritant descalers, it is recommended that gloves are worn and that the eyes should be protected with safety spectacles.
restrictions: Descalers containing hydrochloric acid are not suitable for use with stainless steel surfaces.
Pupils below year 12 must not be permitted to use descalers that are corrosive, though they may use less concentrated products, under supervision.
Descalers must not be mixed with bleach because if a cleaner containing acid is mixed with bleach containing sodium (or calcium) hypochlorite, the toxic gas chlorine will be released.
Therefore, under no circumstances must a descaler be mixed with, or used at the same time as, bleach or other cleaning agents.
disposal: Unwanted descaling liquids should be diluted by adding no more than 100 ml to a bucket of water before flushing down the foul-water drain. Alternatively, they can be neutralised by adding sodium carbonate (washing soda) until the fizzing stops, and then flushed away in any quantity. Empty containers may be added to ordinary waste.
storage: All descalers should be stored away from food areas and in a safe and secure place so that they cannot be taken by pupils without permission and misused.
furtherInformation: It is safest to use a descaling agent containing citric acid or one with the lowest concentration of acid compatible with the task to be performed.
Cooperation with cleaning staff over the methods to be used in food technology areas is essential.
firstAid: Descalers are in the eyes: Wash thoroughly for at least ten minutes with water, holding the eyelids apart. Seek medical attention if irritation persists.
Descalers are swallowed: Give plenty of water and seek medical attention. Do not induce vomiting.
Chlorine is liberated: Remove patient to fresh air and seek medical attention.

Spilt on skin or clothes: Remove contaminated clothing. Wash affected area thoroughly with a large amount of water. If a large area of skin is affected, seek medical attention. Soak contaminated clothing and rinse repeatedly.

riskAssessment: Allergic reaction: True allergic reactions to these detergent mixes are not common but, when they occur, they can be very troublesome to the sufferer.

Irritant: All detergents, by their property of helping to dissolve grease, also remove natural oils from the skin leading to possible dryness, chafing and other dermatological problems, particularly in individuals with sensitive skin. The bleaching agents are also usually irritant.
preStart: Where cleaning agents containing enzymes are used, protection with gloves is essential.

teacher.overview: The use of disinfectants to attempt to destroy microorganisms which may be present on surfaces etc in food technology areas.
teacher.supervision: Set locally from the source restrictions, student maturity, class size and Pukekohe High School procedure.
teacher.training: Confirm competency and local authorisation before use.
hazards: Toxic: Some industrial formulations of clear phenolic disinfectants are toxic.
Harmful: Disinfectants containing some formulations of clear phenolics intended for domestic use are rated harmful.
Corrosive: Certain phenolics, such as ‘Lysol’, are rated as corrosive and so is sodium hypochlorite when purchased at over 10% concentration.

Irritant: Disinfectants containing sodium hypochlorite with between 5 to 10% active chlorine, sodium dichloroisocyanurate, ‘VirKon’ powder and some phenolics (including ‘Jeyes fluid’) are all rated irritant. Formulations containing between 0.2% and 1% formaldehyde (methanal) are also irritant.
riskAssessment: Toxic: No disinfectants labelled toxic are needed in food technology.
Harmful: Concentrated disinfectants labelled harmful, present risks if they are swallowed.
Corrosive: No disinfectants labelled corrosive are needed in food technology.

Irritant: Some disinfectants labelled irritant (most are not) present risks to the skin and eyes. ‘VirKon’ powder and phenolics such as ‘Jeyes Fluid’ should also be kept off skin and away from the eyes and nose.
preStart: Gloves and safety spectacles should be worn if concentrated, harmful disinfectants are handled.
Handling phenolic disinfectants and preparing VirKon solutions also requires the use of gloves and safety spectacles.
safeUse: Gloves and safety spectacles should be worn if concentrated, harmful disinfectants are handled.
Handling phenolic disinfectants and preparing VirKon solutions also requires the use of gloves and safety spectacles.
restrictions: Pupils below year 12 must not be permitted to use disinfectants that are corrosive or toxic except under close personal supervision, though they may use disinfectants that are harmful or irritant.
disposal: Small quantities of disinfectants can be mixed with a bucket-full of water and flushed down the foul-water drain. Solids and empty containers can be added to other solid waste.
storage: All hazardous disinfectants should be stored away from food areas and in a safe place so that they cannot be handled by pupils without permission and misused.
furtherInformation: There are many different brands and types of disinfectant, varying considerably in their ability to destroy microorganisms.
Chlorine-releasers Disinfectants with bleach (sodium hypochlorite) as the active ingredient, eg, ‘Domestos’; ‘Milton’, or sodium dichloroisocyanurate, eg, ‘Presept’, release chlorine in solution.

These should be effective against a wide range of microorganisms (including viruses, if the strength is high enough) but are less suitable for very dirty conditions because they are degraded by organic matter; also they corrode metals.
Bleach solution is recommended for all disinfection involving blood.
Dilute hypochlorite solution is non-tainting and suitable for food preparation areas.
Do not mix chlorine-releasing disinfectants with other cleaning agents.
If the disinfectant in use is one containing sodium hypochlorite or dichloroisocyanurate and is mixed with acids, the toxic gas chlorine will be released.
Therefore, under no circumstances must such disinfectants be mixed with, or used at the same time as, any other cleaning agent.
Chloroxylenols These disinfectants, eg, ‘Dettol’, are not regarded as giving the best protection against a wide range of microorganisms and they are easily inactivated.
They are, however, neither corrosive nor irritant.
Diguanides Disinfectants which contain chlorhexidine, eg, ‘Hibitane’, or chlorhexidine mixed with the QAC cetrimide, eg, ‘Savlon’, are only really useful for skin disinfection.
They should not be used for general disinfection tasks as they have limited activity.
Formaldehyde Formaldehyde (methanal) is very effective in killing microorganisms but it is doubtful whether the concentrations used in cleaning agents is sufficient to do so quickly.
Quaternary Ammonium Disinfectants with QACs as their active ingredient, eg, ‘Dettox’ or ‘Cetavlon’, have a Compounds (QACs) limited activity against microorganisms and are easily inactivated.
They are not and appropriate for general disinfection tasks but are employed for cleaning equipment Ampholytic Surfactants and surfaces within the food and catering industries.
Ampholytic surfactant disinfectants, such as ‘Tego’, have properties and limitations similar to QACs.

Phenolics Clear phenolic disinfectants, eg, ‘Printol’, are active against bacteria and fungi but not viruses; unlike bleach, they are not readily broken down by organic matter, such as food remains or grease.
They are unsuitable for use on any food preparation surface and are now difficult to obtain in sensible quantities.

The use of other phenolic disinfectants is discouraged: black fluids or white fluids, eg, ‘Jeyes Fluid’, ‘Izal’ and especially ‘Lysol’ (because it is toxic and less effective than the others). ‘VirKon’ This powerful disinfectant is supplied as a powder and is effective against bacteria, fungi and viruses.
The powder is rated irritant but, when made up as a 1% solution, is neither toxic nor irritant.
The main active constituent is potassium peroxomonosufate, which works by oxidising the infective material.
It should be used as the powder on blood spills.

Disinfectants are spilt: Remove contaminated clothing. Wash affected area thoroughly with a large amount
on the skin or clothes: of water. Soak contaminated clothing and rinse repeatedly.

teacher.overview: The use of chemical cleaning agents to improve the flow through the drain from a sink and remove stains from the sink itself; many use strong acids or alkalis, others contain enzymes or hypochlorite.
teacher.supervision: Set locally from the source restrictions, student maturity, class size and Pukekohe High School procedure.
teacher.training: Confirm competency and local authorisation before use.
hazards: Corrosive: The majority of cleaners utilise caustic soda or potash (sodium or potassium hydroxide) as their active ingredient but some brands use sulfuric acid instead. (Many brands contain more than 50% active chemical; some even use pure sodium hydroxide pellets or undiluted acid.)
Allergic reaction: Enzyme-based products may provoke a response in some people.
Irritant: Products containing sodium hypochlorite with between 5 to 10% active chlorine or sodium dichloroisocyanurate are rated irritant.
Explosion: Some cleaners contain a mix of sodium hydroxide and powdered aluminium that generates extremely flammable hydrogen gas.
riskAssessment: Corrosive: Brands are corrosive if the concentration is more than 2% sodium or potassium hydroxide or more than 15% sulfuric acid. They present high risks, causing severe damage to the eyes and burns to the skin or alimentary canal, if swallowed. Pellets or strong acid react with water making it hot enough to boil and cause splashes of corrosive chemical.

Allergic reaction: Although much safer than the conventional caustic cleaners, there is a very small chance of an allergic response to the enzymes in these products. As it is impossible to identify in advance those individuals who may be hypersensitive, precautions should be observed.
Irritant: Those products labelled irritant present risks to the skin and eyes.
Explosion: Hydrogen-generating cleaners are used for clearing blocked drains and may present significant risks.
preStart: Care must be taken to avoid splashes of liquid or raising dust when the corrosive cleaners are handled, protecting against inhalation or entry into the eyes.
The skin must be protected by wearing suitable gloves1.
A face shield must be used to protect the eyes when using pellets or liquid cleaners using more than 15% sulfuric acid.
With dilute formulations, safety spectacles should be sufficient.
safeUse: Care must be taken to avoid splashes of liquid or raising dust when the corrosive cleaners are handled, protecting against inhalation or entry into the eyes.
The skin must be protected by wearing suitable gloves1.
A face shield must be used to protect the eyes when using pellets or liquid cleaners using more than 15% sulfuric acid.
With dilute formulations, safety spectacles should be sufficient.
The skin must be protected from any contact with enzymic cleaners by wearing gloves if there is any chance of an allergic reaction.
When using sink or drain cleaners that are labelled irritant, safety spectacles should be worn if there is any risk of splashes to the eyes and gloves should be worn to protect the skin.
All sources of ignition must be removed or extinguished when using cleaners that generate hydrogen.
Marigold Suregrip GO4Y or Blue Nitrile G25B are recommended.
See CLEAPSS guidance leaflet PS 50, Gloves as personal Protective Equipment for a full discussion.
restrictions: Pupils must never be allowed to use corrosive sink cleaners.
Any use to clear blockages must be the responsibility of staff who must read, and follow carefully, the instructions on the package.
disposal: Strong acids and alkalis may not be flushed directly into the drains except when using them for cleaning! Unwanted acid cleaners should be poured slowly into water (eg, a half bucket full for 200 ml of cleaner) while wearing a face shield, apron and gloves. Sodium carbonate (washing soda) can then be added until it stops fizzing. Strongly alkaline cleaners (sodium or potassium hydroxides or strong ammonia) are best disposed of with the help of the science department.
storage: All corrosive sink and drain cleaners should be stored away from food areas and in a safe and secure place so that they cannot be handled by pupils without permission and misused.
firstAid: Alkaline cleaners: Obtain medical attention. Irrigate immediately with water, holding the eyelids apart
are in the eyes: and continue irrigation until the casualty reaches hospital.
Acid cleaners: Wash thoroughly for at least ten minutes with water, holding the eyelids apart. Seek
are in the eyes: medical attention if irritation persists.
Swallowed: Give plenty of water and seek medical attention. Do not induce vomiting.

Spilt on the skin or clothes: Remove contaminated clothing. Wash affected area thoroughly with a large amount of water. If a large area is affected or blistering occurs, seek medical attention. Soak contaminated clothing and rinse repeatedly.

teacher.overview: Cleaning the insides of ovens using powders, liquids, gels, sprays and pads.
teacher.supervision: Set locally from the source restrictions, student maturity, class size and Pukekohe High School procedure.
teacher.training: Confirm competency and local authorisation before use.
hazards: Corrosive: Oven cleaners containing more than 2% sodium / potassium hydroxide are corrosive.
Irritant: Oven cleaners containing between 0.5 to 2% sodium / potassium hydroxide are regarded as irritant.
Allergic reaction: Enzyme-based products may provoke a response in some people.
riskAssessment: Corrosive: Oven cleaners are caustic; those that are most powerful contain high concentrations of (usually) sodium hydroxide and are corrosive. The cleaners may be applied as a thick gel (sometimes using a special applicator), with a pad or as a foam spray. The necessity of having to work in a confined area and reach into crevices and corners increases the risk of accidents during the use of such cleaners. Oven cleaners are easier to apply as a foam but may then be more readily sprayed onto exposed skin or into the eyes with potentially serious effects.
Irritant: Formulations with lower concentrations of active ingredient are safer but nevertheless still irritant to skin and eyes.

Allergic reaction: Although much safer than the conventional caustic cleaners, there is a very small chance of an allergic response to the enzymes in these products. As it is impossible to identify in advance those individuals who may be affected, precautions should be observed.
preStart: Great care must be taken when using all corrosive oven cleaners, particularly those that are sprayed onto surfaces.
The instructions supplied with the cleaners must be followed precisely.
It is wise to apply the cleaning agent at arm’s length and to protect the skin from all contact with the cleaning agent and oven surfaces that have already been treated.
The gloves should be long enough to cover the lower arm and the skin of the upper arm should not be exposed.
safeUse: Great care must be taken when using all corrosive oven cleaners, particularly those that are sprayed onto surfaces.
The instructions supplied with the cleaners must be followed precisely.
It is wise to apply the cleaning agent at arm’s length and to protect the skin from all contact with the cleaning agent and oven surfaces that have already been treated.
The gloves should be long enough to cover the lower arm and the skin of the upper arm should not be exposed.
The eyes must be adequately protected when using caustic cleaners.

Hazardous fumes are unlikely to be produced.

teacher.overview: The use of a conventional oven for initial cooking and reheating of precooked food. See sheet 3.011 for the hazards of food poisoning and 3.023 for heating on hobs.
teacher.supervision: Set locally from the source restrictions, student maturity, class size and Pukekohe High School procedure.
teacher.training: Confirm competency and local authorisation before use.
hazards: Hazard: Burning and scalding Cooking or reheating foods may result in a burn or scald to the skin.
Fire: Overheated food, fats or cooking oil may ignite.
Explosion: Gas that has not ignited presents a potential explosion hazard.

Food poisoning (Infection): Gastrointestinal infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms (particularly E. coli 0157 and Salmonella) and/or their toxic products.
riskAssessment: Risk: Burning and scalding Handling oven shelves and hot containers often result in minor burns and scalds. Cookers with controls at the back present an increased risk. The greatest risk occurs when putting items into, and removing them from, an oven particularly if hot shelves must be moved. When opening oven doors, blasts of hot, moist air / steam can cause involuntary movement and mist up spectacles.
Fire: Oils and fats present the greatest risk of fire in the kitchen. Build up of debris in oven can cause fires.
Explosion: Gas cookers should, if possible, be installed away from windows, otherwise sunlight can make flames invisible or draughts can blow out pilot lights and small flames.

Food poisoning (Infection): While initial cooking destroys microorganisms and toxins, the temperature must be held sufficiently high for long enough to achieve this. Food chilled after cooking may become re-infected or remaining organisms may replicate (slowly) while chilled so that it must again reach a high temperature to ensure safety.
preStart: Correct instruction and appropriate use of oven gloves or cloths should minimise the risk of burns when putting dishes into or removing them from an oven.
Oven gloves must always be used when putting items into, and removing them from, a hot oven.
Oven shelves should be checked to see that they are in the required position, are level on their runners and cannot tip up when pulled out, laden with food.
Care must be taken when opening oven doors, to guard against blasts of hot air.
safeUse: Correct instruction and appropriate use of oven gloves or cloths should minimise the risk of burns when putting dishes into or removing them from an oven.
Oven gloves must always be used when putting items into, and removing them from, a hot oven.
Oven shelves should be checked to see that they are in the required position, are level on their runners and cannot tip up when pulled out, laden with food.
Care must be taken when opening oven doors, to guard against blasts of hot air.
To reduce the dangers of accidents, the number of pupils working at any one time around heating equipment must be controlled.
It is difficult to reduce the risk of fat-pan fires to zero so everyone must be taught how to deal safely with such a fire when it occurs.
Open deep fat frying in not recommended in Food technology.
The oven should be kept clean and free from build up of debris that could cause fires.
Where siting is less than ideal, extra care must be taken to check pilot lights regularly or to confirm that gas has ignited properly.
Chicken and pork are the foods most likely to contain Salmonella while any meat could be contaminated with E. coli 0157 and cooking these foods thoroughly is essential.
Pre-stuffed joints and poultry are sometimes difficult to heat throughout in a conventional oven and testing with a suitable, clean thermometer is advisable.
restrictions: Food should not be heated or reheated while covered with certain plastic films; see sheet 3.019 for more information.
Food should not be heated or reheated while covered with cling film; see sheet 3.019 for more information.
Chilled food should not be left on tables or worktops before reheating: this allows the microorganisms to replicate and increases the risk that they will not be destroyed by the reheating process.
Chilled food should go directly from the refrigerator to the oven.
Cooked foods need to be cooled quickly, ideally using a blast chiller and then refrigerated.

furtherInformation: If food covered with cling film is heated in an oven, it is important to ensure that the film is not touching the food.
Care must be taken not to look too closely at roasting foods in case hot fat splashes into the eyes.
Ensuring adequate heating of foods If cooking in a microwave oven then see sheet 3.027.

If food is to be cooked at all, it is important to cook it thoroughly, following the correct conditions for each heating method and type of food and ensuring that the food is really very hot at the centre.
It is safer to heat food during cooking or reheating until it is too hot and allow it to cool, rather than undercook or under-reheat food.
If food is not piping hot throughout after cooking, bacteria causing gastroenteritis may still be present.
It could be useful to check the settings on a conventional oven with a special oven thermometer from time to time.
Where it is essential to keep cooked food hot for a period before it is consumed, see sheet 3.018.

This cover must stay in place until the pan is cold to prevent re-ignition.
The use of water or the wrong extinguisher can seriously spread the fire with disastrous consequences.

Ensuring adequate heating of foods If food is to be cooked at all, it is important to cook it thoroughly, following the correct conditions for each heating method and type of food and ensuring that the food is really very hot at the centre.
If cooking in a microwave oven (see sheet 3.027), the conditions and standing times recommended by the manufacturer must be observed.
To destroy bacteria during heating, food must reach an internal temperature of at least 70 °C for a minimum of 2 minutes.
Food should normally be prepared just prior to serving; leaving perishable food out at room temperature for more than one hour or keeping food warm for extended periods should be avoided.
Where it is essential to keep cooked food hot for a period before it is consumed, particular care over the temperature must be observed and regular checks of the temperature made.

Reheating foods Liquid foods such as soups, stocks, sauces and gravy provide an ideal breeding ground for rapid microbial growth; such liquids can, however, be preserved by freezing after their preparation.
If not frozen immediately, they should not be kept or reheated.
Cooked food should be reheated only once, whether originally cooked in the home or purchased as a cook / chill product; any left-overs after reheating should be thrown away.
Food should be reheated thoroughly, otherwise any bacteria that may have contaminated the food after the initial cooking or during storage can survive and reproduce.
If bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus have multiplied in the food, they are capable of forming a heat-resistant toxin, so the food may still be unsafe even though it has been thoroughly heated.
Cooked rice is particularly likely to contain spores of Bacillus cereus that have survived the cooking process.

Serious burns to the skin: Seek further medical assistance. Send for an ambulance. Cool the affected area under a running cold tap for ten minutes. Watch for difficulty in breathing or faintness. Gently remove jewellery or watches that might be difficult to remove later if the limb swells. Apply a dry dressing held in place by a cotton wool pad secured with a bandage or adhesive tape if the ambulance has not yet arrived.
Hot fat is splashed: Wash thoroughly for at least ten minutes with water to cool the eye as quickly as
into the eyes: possible. Seek medical attention if irritation persists.

Poisoning is suspected: If a casualty is suffering from nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea with drowsiness or unconsciousness, do not induce vomiting. Provided the casualty is conscious, wash out mouth with water. Obtain medical attention.

teacher.overview: Defrosting foods that are precooked and defrosting food that is to be cooked.
teacher.supervision: Set locally from the source restrictions, student maturity, class size and Pukekohe High School procedure.
teacher.training: Confirm competency and local authorisation before use.
hazards: Food poisoning (Infection): Gastrointestinal infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxic products.
Poisons on food: Contamination of fatty foods wrapped in plastic films with chemicals from the plastic.
riskAssessment: Food poisoning (Infection): Freezing does not kill the organisms causing food poisoning, it stops them from multiplying rapidly. There is a negligible risk with precooked food which is eaten cold (eg, a frozen cake). Frozen meat, particularly poultry, may not reach a temperature high enough to kill Campylobacter or Salmonella during cooking if cooked from frozen. The cooking can then encourage the growth of pathogenic microorganisms in parts of the food.

Food poisoning (Infection): Harmful bacteria require food, moisture, warmth and time to survive and multiply. All reproduce rapidly at temperatures around 37 °C (ie, body temperature), but many can multiply at lower or higher temperatures. Some can do so, although slowly, at temperatures even as low as 5 °C. Some foods are a greater risk than others (see below). Neglect of temperature control may have been the cause of a majority of food poisoning cases in recent years.

Poisons on food: Problems that were identified in the 1970s with PVC-based films have largely been eliminated by changing the formulation of the plastic used. Nevertheless, fatty foods are more likely than others to absorb any chemicals released by plastic packaging. Even in the worst cases, the concentration of such contaminants is likely to be very low and so present no problem.
preStart: It is essential to follow the supplier’s instructions that are printed on frozen poultry.
Should there be no instructions, the bird should be thawed thoroughly by leaving at room temperature for up to 8 hours.
Other meat is usually defrosted by leaving it overnight in a refrigerator.
Prepared dishes are often cooked from frozen but those that have been frozen in a domestic freezer are best defrosted before reheating.
safeUse: It is essential to follow the supplier’s instructions that are printed on frozen poultry.
Should there be no instructions, the bird should be thawed thoroughly by leaving at room temperature for up to 8 hours.
Other meat is usually defrosted by leaving it overnight in a refrigerator.
Prepared dishes are often cooked from frozen but those that have been frozen in a domestic freezer are best defrosted before reheating.
A refrigerator that stores food at a temperature below 5 °C can delay bacterial growth for up to 5 days.
Those foods that are listed below should be kept in such a refrigerator for even short-term storage.
See Further Information for Good practice in safe refrigerator management.
For long-term storage, food should be kept at -18 °C.
Although bacteria will survive at this temperature, they will not be able to multiply until the temperature is raised.
See Further Information for Good practice in safe freezer management.

Although film made from polyethylene or from VDC copolymer plastics, eg, ‘microwave and freezer wrap’, is safer, the advice of the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food was that it is unwise to distinguish between different types of food wrap.

There is no evidence of a health hazard from any type of cling film but little is known of the chemicals that migrate from the plastics into food and so it is sensible to minimise the contact between fatty foods and films.
restrictions: Food that has become defrosted as a result of a power or freezer failure should be disposed of and not eaten.
disposal: Any frozen food that is discovered to be well-past its ‘best-before date’ should be placed in the solid waste.
Frozen or chilled foods past their use-by dates must be disposed of (see 3.034).
storage: Commercially frozen food is given a ‘star rating’ to indicate how long it should be stored in a freezer: 1 week 1 month until ‘best-before date’.
furtherInformation: When shopping, it is best to select chilled and frozen foods last to minimise the amount of time during which the food can warm up in transit.
If possible, also avoid purchasing such foods at times when queues could build up at the check-out.
Pack frozen and chilled foods in separate bags and, wherever possible, use an insulated food bag for transporting such items home to avoid any significant temperature increase.
All chilled and frozen foods must be placed immediately into a well maintained refrigerator or freezer.
It is essential to read and follow thawing instructions on frozen foods thoroughly and carefully.
This will not only be safer but also restores the best flavour and texture.
Items should be placed on a tray, plate or dish that is sufficiently deep to collect any liquid that drips from the thawed product.
Overloading the dish with several frozen items should be avoided because this prolongs the thawing time and results in the food on the outside of the dish thawing first.

While the food is thawing, it should be covered to prevent contamination from the atmosphere and kept in a cool place; although this takes longer, the food will thaw more thoroughly and will be safer.
If defrosting is to be done in a microwave oven, see sheet 3.027.
Thawing times depend on the thickness and mass of foods and many small items, such as fish fillets, burgers and vegetables, may be cooked straight from the frozen state.
Thawed food should not be refrozen unless cooked thoroughly.

Those foods that are a greater risk and therefore need more care include the following. • All meat and poultry products which may be contaminated with food poisoning bacteria. • Raw fish and shellfish are especially likely to harbour bacteria able to multiply at low temperatures and may have come from polluted waters. • Milk, eggs and foods containing them such as cream, custard or mayonnaise that provide an ideal mixture of nutrients needed by multiplying bacteria. • Cooked meat and gravy, soups and stock which are also ideal media for bacteria. • Cooked rice is likely to contain bacterial spores that have survived the cooking process.
If such foods are not cool enough, a small number of bacteria can become millions very quickly.
Good practice in safe refrigerator management 1 Keep the refrigerator door tightly closed, open only when necessary and close it promptly.
2 Keep the refrigerator clean and free from any build-up of ice.
3 Remove old items once use by date has been reached.
4 Fit a thermometer, which can be seen easily and checked daily, on the inside wall or wire shelf 15 cm from the outside edge and half way down the refrigerator.
Temperatures should be between 1 and 4 °C. (There will be a variation of 2 or 3 degrees between different parts of the refrigerator.) 5 Allow cold air to circulate; do not overfill the refrigerator.
6 Follow storage instructions and observe ‘eat-by’ dates on labels.
7 Keep all food covered.
8 Food should be cool before being put into the refrigerator, eg, do not use it to set jelly quickly.
9 Raw food and cooked food must be kept entirely separate to avoid cross-contamination.
10 Raw meat and poultry should be isolated and placed where juices cannot drip onto other food.
11 Fresh fruit and vegetables should be washed before storage in a salad crisper drawer.
12 Food to be stored should be clearly labelled with contents, date of storage and use-by date.
Good practice in safe freezer management 1 Frozen food deteriorates in flavour and texture with time.
How long it should be stored depends on the type of food and the rating of the freezer, usually from 3 months to 1 year.
2 Keep the door or lid tightly closed, open only when necessary and close it promptly.
3 Keep the freezer clean and free from any build-up of ice.
4 Defrost regularly and dispose of any out of date items.
5 Display a freezer thermometer where it can be seen so the reading checked easily (-18 °C).
6 Wrap food adequately (see below), seal, label and date so that it can be used in rotation.
7 Display and follow manufacturers’ instructions on storage times and temperatures.
8 Never refreeze food that has been thawed.
Wrapping foods for storage in refrigerators and freezers Do not use cling film to wrap fatty foods (eg, cheese, butter, cooked meats or cakes / biscuits with chocolate or cream coatings, etc).
Either place the food in containers which are then covered with cling film so that it is not in contact with the food or use sealable containers, plastic bags or aluminium foil instead.
Cling film can be used to wrap non-fatty foods such as most fruit and vegetables.

teacher.overview: Tasting during preparation (for flavour adjustment) and consuming food after preparation and cooking as the end point of the activity. Sensory analysis activities.
teacher.supervision: Set locally from the source restrictions, student maturity, class size and Pukekohe High School procedure.
teacher.training: Confirm competency and local authorisation before use.
hazards: Food poisoning (Infection): Gastrointestinal infection results from eating or hand-to-mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxic products.
Poisons on food: Poisoning which is not an infection results from eating or hand-to-mouth contact with, food containing natural toxic chemicals or contaminants from the environment.
Food contamination: Food may become contaminated during or after preparation by someone carrying an infectious disease.

Allergic reaction: Allergic reactions may develop from exposure to many foods. Some people have become ‘sensitised’, ie, even a very small dose of the allergen then produces the reaction. Substances likely to cause reactions include peanuts, milk, flour (gluten) and food additives.
Food poisoning (Infection): Eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxic products may result in gastro-intestinal infection.
Poisons on food: Poisoning which is not an infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food containing natural toxic chemicals or contaminants from the environment.
riskAssessment: Food poisoning (Infection): Even fresh food of the highest quality should be expected to be carrying organisms that will lead to decay. One purpose of cooking food is to control this process but, if food is not sufficiently fresh when purchased, cooking it may be too late to prevent problems. Careless handling within the kitchen may also lead to contamination, in particular, storing food inappropriately.

Poisons on food: Foods are frequently contaminated with pesticides, fungicides or fertilisers during their production. Even foods that are produced by ‘organic’ methods are not necessarily free of natural poisons.

Food contamination: Tasting food with a dirty spoon may be a source of infection. Similarly, when food is tasted by a group of pupils, shared spoons, forks and dishes may lead to the transmission of microorganisms.
Allergic reaction: Any ‘foreign’ protein may produce an allergic response in sensitive individuals and inadvertent consumption of traces of nuts have been known to cause anaphylactic shock.

Food poisoning (Infection): If high standards of hygiene are not maintained while preparing food, pathogenic microorganisms may be transferred to the food from the handler or from other foods via the work surface or utensils as well as from other foods directly.

Poisons on food: Carelessness or ignorance of the appropriate preparation techniques increases the risk of natural toxins being consumed but items presenting risks are restricted to red kidney beans, green or sprouting parts of potatoes and rhubarb leaves. Chemical residues, eg, from pesticides, may also be present but rarely at significant concentrations.

Allergic reaction: Any ‘foreign’ protein may produce an allergic response in sensitive individuals but simply handling the offending substance is unlikely to produce anything worse than skin irritation. However, inadvertent consumption of traces of nuts have caused anaphylactic shock.
preStart: The highest standards of hygiene must be maintained at all times and particularly when pupils are working closely together in the same area. riskAssessment: Food poisoning (Infection): Bacteria will not multiply in dry foods but they can be introduced by pests and multiply during food preparation. They should not be present in intact cans or other food containers but may enter if the container has been accidentally damaged or once it has been opened. The longer food is kept, the more likely it is to become infested.

Poisons on food: The risks of food becoming contaminated by transfer from other foods or from their environment are greater in storage without adequate segregation. If dry foods are stored with cleaning agents or equipment, the risk of contamination is significant.

Staff should be vigilant for signs of pests.

Proper segregation in storage necessary to prevent contamination.

furtherInformation: The store cupboard for dry foodstuffs should be: • cool, dry, well-ventilated and, if appropriate, well-lit; • designed so that pests have no way of entering; • such that all food can be stored above floor level; • ideally of such a size that similar foods can be placed together with space for an unopened container behind the one in use; • not used for storage of anything else.

teacher.overview: Keeping cooked food warm until it is to be consumed.
teacher.supervision: Set locally from the source restrictions, student maturity, class size and Pukekohe High School procedure.
teacher.training: Confirm competency and local authorisation before use.
hazards: Food poisoning (Infection): Gastrointestinal infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxic products.

Food poisoning (Infection): Gastrointestinal infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms (particularly E. coli 0157 and Salmonella) and/or their toxic products.
riskAssessment: Food poisoning (Infection): Food that is to be eaten hot, but cannot be consumed immediately, may harbour microorganisms which multiply during the period between cooking and eating when the food is still warm.

Food poisoning (Infection): While initial cooking destroys microorganisms and toxins, the temperature must be held sufficiently high for long enough to achieve this. Food chilled after cooking may become re-infected or remaining organisms may replicate (slowly) while chilled so that it must again reach a high temperature to ensure safety.
preStart: It is essential to store the food in such a way that its temperature is raised above 63 °C throughout the period between cooking and consumption.
Steps must be taken to ensure that the heat supply is such that all of the food is maintained at the required temperature.
Regular temperature checks with a food probe should be made.
Chicken and pork are the foods most likely to contain Salmonella while any meat could be contaminated with E. coli 0157 and cooking these foods thoroughly is essential.
safeUse: It is essential to store the food in such a way that its temperature is raised above 63 °C throughout the period between cooking and consumption.
Steps must be taken to ensure that the heat supply is such that all of the food is maintained at the required temperature.
Regular temperature checks with a food probe should be made.
Chicken and pork are the foods most likely to contain Salmonella while any meat could be contaminated with E. coli 0157 and cooking these foods thoroughly is essential.
Pre-stuffed joints and poultry are sometimes difficult to heat throughout in a conventional oven and testing with a suitable, clean thermometer is advisable.
restrictions: If a suitable thermometer is not available to demonstrate that this temperature is being achieved, no attempt should be made to keep food hot in this way.
Food should not be heated or reheated while covered with cling film; see sheet 3.019 for more information.
Chilled food should not be left on tables or worktops before reheating: this allows the microorganisms to replicate and increases the risk that they will not be destroyed by the reheating process.
Chilled food should go directly from the refrigerator to the oven.
Cooked foods need to be cooled quickly, ideally using a blast chiller and then refrigerated.
furtherInformation: It is always recommended that food should be consumed immediately after cooking.
If this is impossible for some reason, it is preferable to cool the food quickly, ideally using a blast chiller, store it in a refrigerator and then reheat thoroughly later.
Advice should be given to pupils on the reheating of dishes prepared in school and then taken home.
It is unusual for in food technology in schools and colleges to need to keep cooked food hot.
However, it is necessary for special projects or occasions when visitors are involved.

Ensuring adequate heating of foods If food is to be cooked at all, it is important to cook it thoroughly, following the correct conditions for each heating method and type of food and ensuring that the food is really very hot at the centre.
If cooking in a microwave oven (see sheet 3.027), the conditions and standing times recommended by the manufacturer must be observed.
To destroy bacteria during heating, food must reach an internal temperature of at least 70 °C for a minimum of 2 minutes.
It is safer to heat food during cooking or reheating until it is too hot and allow it to cool, rather than undercook or under-reheat food.
If food is not piping hot throughout after cooking, bacteria causing gastroenteritis may still be present.
Food should normally be prepared just prior to serving; leaving perishable food out at room temperature for more than one hour or keeping food warm for extended periods should be avoided.
Where it is essential to keep cooked food hot for a period before it is consumed, particular care over the temperature must be observed and regular checks of the temperature made.

Cooked food should be reheated only once, whether originally cooked in the home or purchased as a cook / chill product; any left-overs after reheating should be thrown away.
Food should be reheated thoroughly, otherwise any bacteria that may have contaminated the food after the initial cooking or during storage can survive and reproduce.
If bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus have multiplied in the food, they are capable of forming a heat-resistant toxin, so the food may still be unsafe even though it has been thoroughly heated.
