student.headline: One person at a time. Keep hands clear, secure attachments and unplug before changing parts.
hazards: Moving blades or beaters can cut or trap
Loose hair or clothing can catch
Electrical damage can cause shock
Equipment can move or throw food if used badly
beforeStart: Use the tool only after teacher instruction.
Tie back hair and keep clothing secure.
Check attachments, guards, plug and lead.
Make sure the work area is dry and clear.
dos: Only one student operates the tool at a time.
Hold and use the tool as demonstrated.
Switch off and unplug before fitting, removing or cleaning attachments.
Keep cables away from water and hot surfaces.
donts: Do not touch moving parts.
Do not change attachments while plugged in.
Do not use damaged equipment.
Do not distract someone using a powered tool.
stop: The attachment is loose, jammed or damaged.
The tool behaves unexpectedly.
The plug or cable is damaged.
Someone is cut or receives an electric shock.
student.note: Curated student teaching summary. It does not replace the full teacher RAMS, exact equipment manual or local school procedure.

teacher.overview: The use of hand-held kitchen equipment which comes in several sizes from small battery-powered whisks to machines which really need a stand and table top blenders and smoothie makers
teacher.supervision: Set locally from the source restrictions, student maturity, class size and Pukekohe High School procedure.
teacher.training: Confirm competency and local authorisation before use.
hazards: Electric shock: Damage to the casing of the appliance, the plug or to a mains power cord can present an electric shock hazard. Water inside the appliance can lead to insulation breakdown and to external metal becoming live.
Injury: Sharp cutting surfaces may be hazardous if the equipment is misused or if care is not taken during cleaning or storage.
Tripping: Mains leads that trail across the floor present a tripping hazard.
Dust: Flour dust presents both a health and an allergic reaction hazard.
Food poisoning (Infection): Eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxic products may result in gastro-intestinal infection.
Poisons on food: Poisoning which is not an infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food containing natural toxic chemicals or contaminants from the environment.

Allergic reaction: Allergic reactions may develop from exposure to many foods. Some people have become ‘sensitised’, ie, even a very small dose of the allergen then produces the reaction. Substances likely to cause reactions include peanuts, milk, flour (gluten) and food additives.
riskAssessment: Electric shock: Appliances that are repeatedly moved, plugged in and unplugged are liable to damage which increases this risk. If the power cord is long then it can be damaged by trapping in cupboard doors, by being caught in its own mechanism or by touching hot objects on a hob. Holding the whole machine under a tap to wash cutters or beaters can allow water to enter which may present a serious risk.

Injury: Small grinders, eg, for coffee beans, which often have a top which must be held down to operate the on / off switch, present little risk of injury unless the top is broken and allows a finger to enter. Hand-held mixers have too low a power to cause significant injury with the beaters supplied.
Tripping: If appliances have to be fitted with long leads that trail across the floor, the tripping risk is significant.

Dust: Flour dust has now been given a Workplace Exposure Limit (WEL) which means that the concentration of flour in the air must be kept below 30 mg/m3 (15 min ref period)1 and as far below this as reasonably practicable.

Food poisoning (Infection): If high standards of hygiene are not maintained while preparing food, pathogenic microorganisms may be transferred to the food from the handler or from other foods via the work surface or utensils as well as from other foods directly.

Poisons on food: Carelessness or ignorance of the appropriate preparation techniques increases the risk of natural toxins being consumed but items presenting risks are restricted to red kidney beans, green or sprouting parts of potatoes and rhubarb leaves. Chemical residues, eg, from pesticides, may also be present but rarely at significant concentrations.

Allergic reaction: Any ‘foreign’ protein may produce an allergic response in sensitive individuals but simply handling the offending substance is unlikely to produce anything worse than skin irritation. However, inadvertent consumption of traces of nuts have caused anaphylactic shock.
preStart: Frequent visual checks and regular formal inspections reduce risks of electric shock resulting from damage to a low level.
Users must be taught to remove cutters and beaters (where possible) for cleaning and not to put the whole appliance in the sink or under a tap.
The appliance itself and cutters that cannot be removed must be cleaned with a damp cloth or paper while the appliance is unplugged.

Users must be trained not to push food down the feed tube of a processor with fingers but to use the pushing implement provided and to isolate the machine from the power supply before removing accessories for cleaning.
safeUse: Frequent visual checks and regular formal inspections reduce risks of electric shock resulting from damage to a low level.
Users must be taught to remove cutters and beaters (where possible) for cleaning and not to put the whole appliance in the sink or under a tap.
The appliance itself and cutters that cannot be removed must be cleaned with a damp cloth or paper while the appliance is unplugged.

Users must be trained not to push food down the feed tube of a processor with fingers but to use the pushing implement provided and to isolate the machine from the power supply before removing accessories for cleaning.
Clear instructions must be available.
If long mains leads cannot be avoided, they must be routed so that there is no risk of anyone tripping over them.
If any mixer tends to produce a cloud of flour dust, it should either be fitted with a lid or the method of adding flour to the mix should be chosen to minimise the problem.
Strict adherence to the highest standards of personal hygiene is required (see the Introduction to Part 3).
Every effort must be made to ensure clean working conditions (see 3.003) and to avoid contamination from other foods via utensils (see also 3.011 & 3.024).
Washing is adequate to remove chemical residues from most fruit and vegetables.
The treatment for natural toxins depends on the food.
Rhubarb stalks should have all the leaves removed before cooking as should green and sprouting parts of potatoes.
Red kidney beans must be cooked as thoroughly as during the canning process.
Allergic reactions can only be controlled by awareness of problems and separation of sufferers from their allergens.
restrictions: This type of equipment should be operated by one pupil at a time.
Although food processors are very safe to use, some classes may contain pupils who are too disruptive to be trusted with such equipment.
Persons suffering from sickness, diarrhoea, colds, coughs or other infections should not prepare food for consumption by others.
disposal: See 3.034. The Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment Regulations 2006 (the WEEE Regulations) apply.
storage: Any tool that has the potential to be misused should be stored in a secure place.
furtherInformation: When using electric carving knives, it is important to follow guidance from the manufacturer and only use with foods that are suitable for cutting with this equipment.
It is also important to ensure that the knife is not connected to the power when inserting or removing the blades.
Remember never to wash the blades in water while still attached to the motor.
After removal, the blades should be washed with care.
The blades are self-sharpening by friction during use and should not be sharpened manually.
As with food mixers etc, only one student at a time should attempt to use the equipment.

International food safety requirements Under the auspices of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, the Codex Alimentarius Commission has created a series of guidelines, standards and other recommendations to ensure food hygiene internationally.
These include a Recommended International Code of Practice - General Principles of Food Hygiene that uses a Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) system for its application.
If this system is followed, the foodstuffs that now travel from all parts of the world to our shops will meet common standards for safety, wholesomeness and safe levels of chemical contaminants.
Preventing contamination of food after purchase Avoid putting cooked or ready-to-eat foods on to a surface that has just had raw food prepared on it.
Raw food, especially meat and fish, is more likely to have bacteria on it than cooked food.
Cheese should therefore not come into direct contact with meat or surfaces where meat has been prepared.
Raw and cooked foods should be kept separate and where possible and appropriate, covered or wrapped.
Avoid adding freshly-prepared food to items prepared previously or putting freshly-prepared food into unwashed containers.
Wash poultry, fish and offal thoroughly in clean, cold, running water.
Keep these items cool and covered in between preparation processes, so far as possible.
Wash fruit, vegetables and salads in clean, cold, running water and keep cool in clean, covered containers until required.
Throw away old food wrappings such as foil, cling film or polythene bags and use fresh, clean, food wrappings.

Do not wrap fatty foods with cling film; chemicals may leach out of the film into the food. (See 3.019 for more information.) Look out for the appearance of insect pests, particularly in food cupboards, and deal with infestations before they build up; animals carry bacteria that can contaminate food preparation areas and work surfaces.
Students should be advised to keep pet animals at home out of the kitchen and away from food storage and preparation areas.
Change and wash tea towels and dish cloths daily, otherwise bacteria can build up and contaminate any surface with which the cloths come into contact.
Students should be advised to exercise special care and caution after handling domestic washing at home.
Soiled washing can spread bacteria, especially if a family member has an infection or diarrhoea.
They should be instructed never to sort out soiled washing on surfaces where food is prepared and always to wash hands after handling soiled washing.
firstAid: Flour dust is in the eyes: Wash thoroughly for at least ten minutes with water to prevent scratching of the eye. Seek medical attention if irritation persists.
Cuts: If cuts are minor, ie, of a sort which casualties would normally treat themselves, the wound should be washed clean and a small, sterilised dressing applied.

Electric shock: Send for a first aider immediately. Taking care for your own safety, break contact by switching off or pulling out the plug. If it is necessary to move the casualty without switching off the supply, use a broom handle or wooden window pole or wear rubber gloves. If the casualty is unconscious and not breathing, check that the airways are clear and begin artificial ventilation. Send for an ambulance. If a trained first aider does not arrive quickly and the casualty has no pulse, consider carrying out cardio-pulmonary resuscitation.

Poisoning is suspected: If a casualty is suffering from nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea with drowsiness or unconsciousness, do not induce vomiting. Provided the casualty is conscious, wash out mouth with water. Obtain medical attention.
Anaphylactic shock: If the patient suffers from impaired breathing and a rapid pulse, they may be going

(major allergic reaction): into anaphylactic shock. Seek further medical help immediately. Check to see if the patient is carrying an Epi-Pen or syringe of adrenaline; if so then help them to administer it. Call an ambulance and prop the patient in a sitting position.

student.headline: A pressure cooker holds very hot steam under pressure. Use it only after training and never open it while pressurised.
hazards: Pressurised steam can cause serious scalds
A blocked vent can make pressure rise too high
Hot metal surfaces can burn
Opening the cooker too early can release hot contents suddenly
beforeStart: Get teacher permission and follow the exact cooker instructions.
Check the cooker, seal, vent and safety parts are clean and in good condition.
Add the correct amount of food and water.
Know how the pressure indicator works.
dos: Stay with the cooker and watch or listen for normal pressure release.
Use oven gloves when handling hot parts.
Follow the correct cooling and pressure-release method.
Wait until the cooker shows it is back at normal pressure before opening.
donts: Never force the lid open.
Never remove the weight or pressure regulator while the cooker is pressurised.
Do not let the cooker boil dry.
Do not use a damaged or uninspected pressure cooker.
stop: The pressure indicator or vent does not behave normally.
Steam escapes from the wrong place.
The cooker is damaged, leaking or making unusual sounds.
You are not sure the pressure has fully released.
student.note: Curated student teaching summary. It does not replace the full teacher RAMS, exact equipment manual or local school procedure.

teacher.overview: General use of domestic-type pressure cookers.
teacher.supervision: Set locally from the source restrictions, student maturity, class size and Pukekohe High School procedure.
teacher.training: Confirm competency and local authorisation before use.
hazards: Explosion: Failure of a pressure cooker in use, causing the explosive release of its contents.
Overpressure: The operation of a safety pressure release system can present a hazard from escaping steam and the contents of the cooker.
Burns and Scalds: Hot surfaces and the sudden release of steam producing scalds.

Food poisoning (Infection): Gastrointestinal infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms (particularly E. coli 0157 and Salmonella) and/or their toxic products.
riskAssessment: Explosion: Pressure cookers have been known to fail (near normal working pressure) at the points where the handles are attached or as a result of fracture of the lid clamps. Both events are rare and the initial cracks probably would not have been discovered by even an expert inspection.

Overpressure: In use, a pressure cooker should release steam gently. If the outlet becomes blocked by food being cooked or by part of a container, the pressure and temperature rises. A safety device, which is usually a fusible plug, should then operate to release the pressure but, in so doing, the contents boil and may emerge as a scalding jet.

Burns and Scalds: Failure of the pressure regulating system or of the rubber sealing ring are possible causes of sudden release of steam but the most likely cause is the premature release of the lid or removal of weights before pressure has fallen. The metal surface of the pressure cooker gets hot in use and could cause burns if touched.

Food poisoning (Infection): While initial cooking destroys microorganisms and toxins, the temperature must be held sufficiently high for long enough to achieve this. Food chilled after cooking may become re-infected or remaining organisms may replicate (slowly) while chilled so that it must again reach a high temperature to ensure safety.
preStart: Regular inspection under the regulations (see Further Information overleaf) will limit the risk of explosion.
For full guidance see CLEAPSS Guide L214 (parts a to d), Examining Autoclaves, Pressure Cookers and Model Steam Engines.
Instruction should be given in the use of pressure cookers.
Manufacturer’s instructions should be followed at all times.
safeUse: Regular inspection under the regulations (see Further Information overleaf) will limit the risk of explosion.
For full guidance see CLEAPSS Guide L214 (parts a to d), Examining Autoclaves, Pressure Cookers and Model Steam Engines.
Instruction should be given in the use of pressure cookers.
Manufacturer’s instructions should be followed at all times.
When using the cooker, constant attention to the sound of escaping steam and/or inspection of the indicator or gauge is required to ensure that the pressure does not become too high.
After operation of the pressure release, protection of the hand and arm may be necessary in order to approach the cooker and turn off the supply of heat.
The risk of scalds will be reduced if the manufacturer’s instructions (see Restrictions overleaf) are followed carefully when cooling and releasing the lid after use.
Oven gloves must be used when handling a hot cooker or the pressure-regulating system.
Supervision at this stage is recommended.
Chicken and pork are the foods most likely to contain Salmonella while any meat could be contaminated with E. coli 0157 and cooking these foods thoroughly is essential.
Pre-stuffed joints and poultry are sometimes difficult to heat throughout in a conventional oven and testing with a suitable, clean thermometer is advisable.
restrictions: The cooker must not be opened nor the weights removed when the internal pressure is still high.

After cooking is completed, the manufacturer’s instructions on cooling must be followed; usually these require the cooker to cool naturally until an indicator shows that the inside has returned to atmospheric pressure.
Use It is important to ensure that adequate quantities of water have been added, bearing in mind the cooking time.
Boiling dry is often the cause of distortion or ‘doming’ of the base which may require the cooker to be failed when the safety inspection is carried out.
Manufacturer’s instructions should always be followed.
Food should not be heated or reheated while covered with cling film; see sheet 3.019 for more information.
Chilled food should not be left on tables or worktops before reheating: this allows the microorganisms to replicate and increases the risk that they will not be destroyed by the reheating process.
Chilled food should go directly from the refrigerator to the oven.
Cooked foods need to be cooled quickly, ideally using a blast chiller and then refrigerated.
storage: After use, it is necessary to wash the pressure cooker thoroughly, particularly cleaning the weight support and gasket if soiled with food. With cookers that have a ‘ready-to-serve’ indicator in the safety valve, this must be free-moving and not blocked with food debris. The cooker must be stored completely dry; residual moisture may accelerate pitting of the internal surface.
furtherInformation: Under the requirements of the Pressure Systems Safety Regulations (2000)1, it is necessary for the owners or users of pressure cookers, in their places of work, to make arrangements for a regular inspection of these items against a suitable written scheme of examination.
See the CLEAPSS guide L214 parts a to d Examining Autoclaves, Pressure Cookers and Model Steam Engines.

An annual safety check will normally be sufficient, unless the items are in very frequent use, eg, every few weeks, in which case it may be appropriate to make a formal examination more often. (Although it is sensible to give pressure cookers at home a safety check, there is no legal requirement that this should happen.) Under the Regulations, the examination of pressure cookers should be conducted by a ‘competent’ person and it is the employer’s responsibility to decide who this should be.

Staff in a food technology department may find that their employer has chosen to use the services of an insurance company surveyor to carry out the examinations, often along with the school boilers and equipment in the science department, although there is no requirement that an insurance company is used.
The costs of this service may, however, be prohibitive.

Employers may, therefore, have chosen to appoint a competent individual to carry out the examinations of equipment in all its establishments, or to authorise an appropriate, competent person in an establishment to carry out the safety checks.
It should be noted that the 1999 revision of the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations state that a competent employee is to be preferred.

Ensuring adequate heating of foods If food is to be cooked at all, it is important to cook it thoroughly, following the correct conditions for each heating method and type of food and ensuring that the food is really very hot at the centre.
If cooking in a microwave oven (see sheet 3.027), the conditions and standing times recommended by the manufacturer must be observed.
To destroy bacteria during heating, food must reach an internal temperature of at least 70 °C for a minimum of 2 minutes.
It is safer to heat food during cooking or reheating until it is too hot and allow it to cool, rather than undercook or under-reheat food.
If food is not piping hot throughout after cooking, bacteria causing gastroenteritis may still be present.
Food should normally be prepared just prior to serving; leaving perishable food out at room temperature for more than one hour or keeping food warm for extended periods should be avoided.
Where it is essential to keep cooked food hot for a period before it is consumed, particular care over the temperature must be observed and regular checks of the temperature made.

Reheating foods Liquid foods such as soups, stocks, sauces and gravy provide an ideal breeding ground for rapid microbial growth; such liquids can, however, be preserved by freezing after their preparation.
If not frozen immediately, they should not be kept or reheated.
Cooked food should be reheated only once, whether originally cooked in the home or purchased as a cook / chill product; any left-overs after reheating should be thrown away.
Food should be reheated thoroughly, otherwise any bacteria that may have contaminated the food after the initial cooking or during storage can survive and reproduce.
If bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus have multiplied in the food, they are capable of forming a heat-resistant toxin, so the food may still be unsafe even though it has been thoroughly heated.
Cooked rice is particularly likely to contain spores of Bacillus cereus that have survived the cooking process.
firstAid: Burns to the skin: Cool the affected area under a running cold tap for ten minutes.

Serious burns to the skin: Send for an ambulance. Cool the affected area under a running cold tap for ten minutes. Watch for difficulty in breathing or faintness. Gently remove jewellery or watches that might be difficult to remove later if the limb swells. Apply a dry dressing held in place by a cotton wool pad secured with a bandage or adhesive tape if the ambulance has not yet arrived. For details of the Regulations and the Approved Code of Practice that gives guidance on their interpretation, see Safety of Pressure Systems, L122, HSE Books, ISBN 071761767X.

Poisoning is suspected: If a casualty is suffering from nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea with drowsiness or unconsciousness, do not induce vomiting. Provided the casualty is conscious, wash out mouth with water. Obtain medical attention.

hazards: Food poisoning (Infection): Gastrointestinal infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxic products.
Poisons on food: Poisoning which is not an infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact, with food containing natural toxic chemicals or contaminants from the environment.
Out-of-date foods: Few food-packaging methods eliminate all microorganisms or enzymes that can change food; they usually slow down the effects.
riskAssessment: Food poisoning (Infection): If care is not taken in purchasing or selecting food items, there is a possibility that the food may have been contaminated or be carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxins, resulting in infections when the food is consumed.

Poisons on food: The risks of food becoming contaminated by transfer from other foods or from a dirty environment are greater in shops without adequate segregation of different food types. Carelessness or ignorance of the appropriate preparation techniques increases the risk of natural toxins being consumed but items presenting risks are restricted to red kidney beans, green or sprouting parts of potatoes and rhubarb leaves.

Out-of-date foods: Foods that have passed a ‘sell-by date’ or ‘use-by date’ are likely to have a greater risk of infection of the consumer than fresh foods. (See Further Information overleaf for comments on ‘best-before dates’.)
preStart: Fresh foods, including eggs, should be purchased only from reputable shops with good hygiene standards (see Further Information overleaf) and which are popular, so ensuring a rapid turnover of stock.
Traces of pesticides or polluting chemicals may remain on fruit and vegetables, which should be segregated in shops and washed off before consumption.
Dry red kidney beans must be well cooked to destroy their toxins.
Potatoes must be prepared by having green parts and ‘eyes’ removed.
safeUse: Fresh foods, including eggs, should be purchased only from reputable shops with good hygiene standards (see Further Information overleaf) and which are popular, so ensuring a rapid turnover of stock.
Traces of pesticides or polluting chemicals may remain on fruit and vegetables, which should be segregated in shops and washed off before consumption.
Dry red kidney beans must be well cooked to destroy their toxins.
Potatoes must be prepared by having green parts and ‘eyes’ removed.
Only rhubarb stalks should be cooked and eaten.
Packaged foods should always be checked for a future ‘sell-by date’, particularly if they are not to be consumed on the day of purchase.
restrictions: Food in the following situations should be rejected: • unwrapped foods from shelves very close to the floor; • food in damaged, ‘blown’ or rusty tins or containers and vacuum packs with suspect seams; • food that has obviously been mishandled, shows even the slightest evidence of unwanted mould or is past its ‘sell-by date’; • green potatoes or those in a pack size such that they can not be consumed fairly swiftly; • fatty foods such as cheese or pastries that have been wrapped in ‘cling film’. (See 3.019 for more information.)
storage: See 3.017, 3.018, 3.019 & 3.020. If pupils bring in food for food technology work, there should be proper storage arrangements available, both before and after the time for the lesson. The problems of storage of food prior to a lesson can be reduced if the school or college supplies the materials from a central stock.
furtherInformation: Stores with good hygiene standards can be recognised by: • good organisation, eg, loose fruit and vegetables being displayed well away from flowers, fish, meat, dairy and delicatessen items; • being obviously clean (no spills evident in food cabinets or on the floor); • having good lighting; • having hand-washing facilities; • having special facilities for handling raw and cooked foods, ie: separate slicers, boards and small utensils for all different types of foods as well as cooked food products; • proper storage for frozen and chilled foods, ie, with cartons evenly stacked and not above the load line in an open-topped freezer, and by staff handling food: • wearing clean overalls; • having their hair tied back and covered; • wearing minimum jewellery; • having short, clean fingernails with no nail varnish; • being free from coughs, colds and similar infections; • having cuts covered with a food-standard (blue) waterproof dressing; • using tongs or gloves and paper or film to ensure that their hands do not come into direct contact with food.
Foods with ‘best-before’ dates ‘Best-before’ dates on food indicate how long the food is expected to be at its best, ie, having a good flavour and texture.
After this date, the foods are not necessarily ‘unsafe’ to eat.
firstAid: Poisoning is suspected: If a casualty is suffering from nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea with drowsiness or unconsciousness, do not induce vomiting. Provided the casualty is conscious, wash out mouth with water. Obtain medical attention.

hazards: Burns: Hot surfaces may result in a burn or scald to the skin.
Fire: Overheated food, fats or cooking oil may ignite.
Entanglement: Hair, hands and clothing can become entangled in moving parts.
Electric shock: With any electric equipment there is a danger of electric shock.
riskAssessment: Burns: Handling oven shelves and hot containers often result in minor burns and scalds. The greatest risk occurs when putting items into, and removing them from the oven.
Fire: Oils and fats present the greatest risk of fire in the kitchen. Build up of debris in oven can cause fires.
Entanglement: As moving parts are partly exposed, entanglement is possible.
Electric shock: If properly installed by a qualified electrician then this risk should be minimal. Tunnel ovens should be correctly installed with an appropriate fused switch-disconnector.
preStart: All teachers and pupils need adequate training in the use of tunnel ovens prior to use.

The equipment installed should be of a type where the external casing temperature does not cause burns if touched.
Suitable protective equipment should be provided, eg: oven gloves.
safeUse: All teachers and pupils need adequate training in the use of tunnel ovens prior to use.

The equipment installed should be of a type where the external casing temperature does not cause burns if touched.

furtherInformation: Tunnel ovens often require a current supply in excess of 13 amps and will need to be directly connected to a suitable fused switch-disconnector.

teacher.overview: The disposal of food waste including cooked and uncooked material. Disposal of unwanted / irreparable equipment.
teacher.supervision: Set locally from the source restrictions, student maturity, class size and Pukekohe High School procedure.
teacher.training: Confirm competency and local authorisation before use.
hazards: Encouraging pests: Disposing of waste food unhygienically encourages pests that may then contaminate food.
Injury: Irreparable equipment from knives to food mixers may constitute a hazard to persons handling waste.
riskAssessment: Encouraging pests: Work in food technology inevitably generates quantities of food wastes that may pose a hazard if pests such as flies, cockroaches or rodents can gain access. These can transfer bacteria to items of food in storage areas or left uncovered during food preparation, causing food poisoning. Handling a dirty refuse bin and dirty lid can spread bacteria to the hands and so onto food, if good personal hygiene is not observed.
Injury: Any sharp object placed in ordinary refuse can cause injury to cleaners or waste disposal operatives.
preStart: Separate bins should be used for food waste and other wastes.
These must be easy to clean and always fitted with a lid that should preferably be foot-operated.
Each bin should be lined with a plastic bag of suitable size and a new one used every time the bin is emptied.
The bin must be kept clean, especially the lid; the bin should be washed and dried thoroughly every time it is emptied.
safeUse: Separate bins should be used for food waste and other wastes.
These must be easy to clean and always fitted with a lid that should preferably be foot-operated.
Each bin should be lined with a plastic bag of suitable size and a new one used every time the bin is emptied.
The bin must be kept clean, especially the lid; the bin should be washed and dried thoroughly every time it is emptied.
Hands must be washed thoroughly after touching the inside of the bin or its contents.
Sharp, pointed or damaged tools and broken crockery should be placed in a tough container that is sealed before placing it in a dustbin.
restrictions: Much of the electrical equipment in food technology rooms and in other departments comes under the Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment Regulations 2006 (the WEEE Regulations) for disposal.
In practice, in most schools the site staff will arrange for the collection and disposal of such equipment.
The CLEAPSS guidance leaflet PS 77, The WEEE Regulations, gives further of what is required.
disposal: of unwanted / irreparable equipment. HAZARDS Encouraging pests Disposing of waste food unhygienically encourages pests that may then contaminate food. Injury Irreparable equipment from knives to food mixers may constitute a hazard to persons handling waste.

RISK ASSESSMENT Encouraging pests Work in food technology inevitably generates quantities of food wastes that may pose a hazard if pests such as flies, cockroaches or rodents can gain access. These can transfer bacteria to items of food in storage areas or left uncovered during food preparation, causing food poisoning. Handling a dirty refuse bin and dirty lid can spread bacteria to the hands and so onto food, if good personal hygiene is not observed. Injury Any sharp object placed in ordinary refuse can cause injury to cleaners or waste disposal operatives.

CONTROL MEASURES Separate bins should be used for food waste and other wastes. These must be easy to clean and always fitted with a lid that should preferably be foot-operated. Each bin should be lined with a plastic bag of suitable size and a new one used every time the bin is emptied. The bin must be kept clean, especially the lid; the bin should be washed and dried thoroughly every time it is emptied. Hands must be washed thoroughly after touching the inside of the bin or its contents. Sharp, pointed or damaged tools and broken crockery should be placed in a tough container that is sealed before placing it in a dustbin.

RESTRICTIONS Much of the electrical equipment in food technology rooms and in other departments comes under the Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment Regulations 2006 (the WEEE Regulations) for disposal. In practice, in most schools the site staff will arrange for the collection and disposal of such equipment. The CLEAPSS guidance leaflet PS 77, The WEEE Regulations, gives further of what is required.

Disposal Refuse must not be allowed to accumulate in food rooms and should not be left there overnight. As soon as possible, food waste must be moved to the bin used for kitchen waste, which itself should be covered to exclude pests. Increased use of composting will be encouraged. Irreparable electrical goods will have to go to a recycling centre - many local authorities have schemes now.
furtherInformation: Waste-disposal units Some sinks in food technology may have waste-disposal units fitted.
These electrical devices are built into the waste pipe and macerate waste so that it can be flushed away down the foul-water drain.
Water authorities do not encourage the fitting of these units now but there is no prohibition on their use.
They are designed so that fingers cannot reach the cutters but the handles of teaspoons or other narrow implements can pass through the grill into the macerating region.
Clearly, care is needed to avoid damage to either spoons or the unit itself.
See CLEAPSS guidance leaflet PS 31, Disposal of Waste in Design & Technology for a summary of the present legal position.
firstAid: Dust is in the eyes: Wash thoroughly for at least ten minutes with water to prevent scratching of the eye. Seek medical attention if irritation persists.

Moulds: Mould fungi cause food spoilage and produce toxic metabolites (mycotoxins including aflotoxin) which are — — harmful when eaten. Aflotoxin has been associated particularly with mouldy cereals and nuts. The presence of mould, which resembles cotton wool, on food is often an indication that the food may be contaminated with other microorganisms. Moulds can develop on any suitable nutrient base providing sufficient moisture, and can grow over a wide range of temperatures. They spread by forming spores, which are released into the air and if they fall on a favourable environment, such as food, germinate and grow to produce a new colony. ‘At risk’ foods include poorly stored dried fruit (figs), bread, beans and nuts but any food may become contaminated.

Parasites in food: The only significant risk is from toxoplasmosis; other parasites, such as tapeworms, should not be a problem if — — food is obtained from reputable sources. Infection is most hazardous to those in the ‘at risk’ groups, particularly young children and pregnant women. The parasite can spread to humans in undercooked meat or raw meat and raw vegetables which have been contaminated with infected cat faeces or cat litter. The parasite is found in many animals but can only reproduce successfully in the cat’s gut.

Natural toxins: Some food plants contain harmful chemicals, eg, rhubarb and tomato, but the quantities are very small in the — — parts of the plant that are normally eaten. The bean Phaseolus vulgaris, often called the red kidney bean, haricot bean or french bean among other common names, contains a poison which is, however, broken down by heat. Inadequately cooked beans may still be toxic. Solanine builds up in green or sprouting potatoes; if taken in large amounts it leads to gastro-intestinal pain, diarrhoea and could ultimately be fatal. Great care must be exercised if food from the garden or the wild is chosen; particularly guard against mistaken identity when selecting leaves, roots and berries. sources.title: Blast chillers
sources.process: Use of commercial blast chillers to reduce the temperature of food quickly.

hazards.label: Electric shock
hazards.detail: Any electrically powered item presents a shock risk if it is damaged.

hazards.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
hazards.detail: Gastrointestinal infection results from eating, or hand to mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxic products.

riskAssessment.label: Electric shock
riskAssessment.detail: With all electrical equipment there is a risk of electric shock. However blast chillers should be installed by a qualified electrician / plumber and have an appropriately fused switch-disconnect or if hard wired an isolating plug. If the appliance’s rating requires one it should also have a ventilation extraction system. Correct installation and regular maintenance checks reduce the shock risk to minimal.

riskAssessment.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
riskAssessment.detail: Harmful bacteria require food, moisture, warmth and time to survive and multiply. All reproduce rapidly at temperatures around 37 °C (ie, body temperature) but many can multiply at lower or higher temperatures. By blast chilling the risk of bacterial reproduction is considerably reduced.

controlMeasures: The blast chiller should be included in a regular planned maintenance programme and also be part of regular visual checks by a competent person at suitable frequencies to identify any faults that require maintenance to reduce the risk of incorrect operation. Manufacturers instructions should be followed at all times. Only suitable ingredients or foods should be put into the blast chiller. Protective gloves should be worn when removing cold items from the chiller.
disposal: For disposal see 3.034.
furtherInformation: Blast chillers should be included in a regular planned maintenance programme and also be part of regular visual checks by a competent person at suitable frequencies to identify any faults that require maintenance to reduce the risk of incorrect operation.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Freezer burns to the skin
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Run affected area under tepid running water for 10 minutes. Cover with a dry dressing. If severe seek further medical advice.

sources.title: Chemical testing of food
sources.process: Tests to identify the presence of sugars, starch, proteins, fats and vitamin C.

hazards.label: Corrosive
hazards.detail: Solutions of sodium hydroxide at sufficient strength and Millon’s reagent are corrosive.

hazards.label: Toxic
hazards.detail: Millon’s reagent contains toxic components.

hazards.label: Harmful

hazards.label: Irritant

controlMeasures: Food chemical testing is best done in a properly equipped Science laboratory with specialist science technician help. The corrosive and toxic risks can be avoided by using alternatives. Solutions should be prepared by a trained technician wearing gloves and eye protection. Those using irritant solutions should wear eye protection. Whenever ethanol is used, all naked flames and pilot lights in the vicinity should be extinguished.
restrictions: Millon’s reagent should not be used by pupils or students below year 12. Fehling’s solutions and Clinitest tablets should not be used by those below year 9 (see over). All the other tests are suitable for use by responsible pupils of year 7 & above.
disposal: Small quantities of reagents after tests may be diluted with lots of water and flushed into the foul-water drain. (See PS 31, Disposal of Waste in Design & Technology.)
storage: All of these test reagents should be stored in a secure place, away from food. If more than 500 ml of ethanol is kept, it should be in a cabinet designed for highly flammable liquids.

sources.title: Cleaning activities: general
sources.process: General cleaning activities.

hazards.label: Allergic reaction
hazards.detail: Some agents contain substances that produce allergic reactions.

hazards.label: Toxic or harmful
hazards.detail: Some agents contain substances that are toxic or harmful.

hazards.label: Corrosive
hazards.detail: Some agents contain substances that are corrosive.

hazards.label: Irritant
hazards.detail: Some agents contain substances that are irritant.

hazards.label: Flammable
hazards.detail: Some agents contain substances that are flammable or highly flammable.

riskAssessment.label: Allergic reaction
riskAssessment.detail: Many people are aware of allergic reactions to some substances or groups of substances. Some people have become ‘sensitised’, ie, even a very small dose of the allergen then produces the reaction. Substances likely to cause sensitisation are identified by risk phrases R42 & 43.

riskAssessment.label: Toxic or harmful
riskAssessment.detail: Agents presenting these risks are identified by hazard warnings that may vary with different formulations of the same substance.

riskAssessment.label: Corrosive
riskAssessment.detail: Agents presenting these risks are identified by hazard warnings.

riskAssessment.label: Irritant
riskAssessment.detail: Agents presenting these risks are identified by hazard warnings.

riskAssessment.label: Flammable
riskAssessment.detail: Cleaners may contain flammable components but a greater risk is presented by

riskAssessment.label: or highly flammable
riskAssessment.detail: preparations applied as aerosols: the propellant is often highly flammable.

controlMeasures: Training in the safe use of cleaning agents is required by all staff likely to use them. Simple allergic reactions (dermatitis) can be prevented by the use of gloves or by avoiding the agent. Once sensitisation has occurred, it is difficult to avoid the reaction other than by a change of job. It is essential to read the label on the container to ascertain the level of risk and the precautions required to control it. Gloves and eye protection must be worn when using any agent with ‘corrosive’ on the label. An irritant agent should be handled with gloves. If possible, the use of cleaning agents in aerosol spray cans should be avoided but, if used, all naked flames should be extinguished. Care should be taken to see that the contents are not sprayed into the eyes or where they will be inhaled.
restrictions: The separate sheets describe restrictions in the use of certain cleaning agents, where relevant. Because of the possibility of misuse and materials being sprayed into eyes or flames, it would probably be advisable to restrict the use of pressurised, aerosol cans and other sprays to responsible pupils in year 11 and above.
disposal: Unwanted cleaning liquids may be diluted and flushed away down the foul-water drain so long as the acidity / alkalinity is adjusted to a pH between 5.5 and 9. Empty containers should be rinsed out before placing them in the refuse. Empty aerosol cans should not be incinerated as the residual propellant may explode.
storage: All cleaning agents containing hazardous substances must be stored adequately, away from food areas, so that they cannot be misused. The cupboard should be locked and labelled. Aerosol cans must be stored away from sources of heat (ie, below 50 °C).
furtherInformation: It is necessary to wash all work surfaces thoroughly and regularly, on every day that practical work with food is done, using hot water and detergent. The inside of the refrigerator and shelves of food storage cupboards should also be washed before drips or spills accumulate, at least once each week. After washing, the surfaces should be dried with a clean, dry cloth or disposable paper towel. Wet surfaces are a potential breeding ground for bacteria. See individual sheets 3.004 to 3.009. Co-operation with cleaning staff over the methods to be used in food technology areas is essential.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Cleaning agents are
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Obtain medical attention. Irrigate immediately with water, holding eyelids apart and

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: sprayed into the eyes
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: continue until the patient reaches hospital.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Allergic reaction
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: If patients show anxiety, red, blotchy skin, swelling of the face and neck and puffiness around the eyes, they could be suffering from a serious allergic reaction. Call an ambulance and prop such a patient in a sitting position in case breathing problems develop.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Anaphylactic shock
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: If patients suffer from impaired breathing and also has a rapid pulse, they may be

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: (major allergic reaction)
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: going into anaphylactic shock. Check to see if the patients are carrying an Epi-Pen or syringe of adrenaline; if so help them to administer it. Call an ambulance and prop such a patient in a sitting position.

sources.title: Cleaning agents for food handling areas: bleaches
sources.process: Cleaning operations to remove stains using liquids, powders or tablet cleaners.

hazards.label: Corrosive
hazards.detail: Bleaching solutions containing sodium hypochlorite [sodium chlorate(I)] with more than 10% active chlorine and bleaching powder containing calcium hypochlorite [calcium chlorate(I)] are rated corrosive.

hazards.label: Irritant
hazards.detail: Bleaching solutions containing sodium hypochlorite (with between 5 and 10% active chlorine) or hydrogen peroxide and bleach tablets containing sodium dichloroisocyanurate are rated irritant. Powders containing sodium perborate are also irritant.

riskAssessment.label: Corrosive
riskAssessment.detail: Solutions classified as corrosive are very hazardous, causing severe damage to the eyes and burns to the skin or alimentary canal, if swallowed. Most ‘concentrated’ bleach solutions available commercially are, however, not so strong as this. Calcium hypochlorite is very dangerous to the skin and eyes. It readily raises dust that could be inhaled or damage the eyes.

riskAssessment.label: Irritant
riskAssessment.detail: Bleaches employing hydrogen peroxide as the active ingredient will not usually be sufficiently concentrated to present a major risk in normal use but should be treated as irritant. ‘Bleach’ powders containing sodium perborate will be irritant to the eyes.

controlMeasures: Bleaches that are corrosive require the user to wear a face shield and gloves when dispensing a liquid. Gloves are sufficient when using a scouring powder1. Bleaches that are labelled irritant require the eyes to be protected with safety spectacles and gloves should be worn to protect the skin.
Marigold Suregrip GO4Y or Blue Nitrile G25B are recommended. See CLEAPSS publication PS 50, Gloves as personal Protective Equipment for a full discussion.
restrictions: Pupils below year 12 should not be permitted to use bleach solutions or powders that are corrosive, though they may use diluted solutions under supervision. Do not mix bleach with other cleaning agents
disposal: Small quantities of bleaches can be mixed with a bucket-full of water and flushed down the foul-water drain. Solids and empty containers can be added to other solid waste.
storage: All bleaches should be stored away from food areas and in a safe and secure place so that they cannot be taken by pupils without permission and misused. As hypochlorite and hydrogen peroxide bleaches deteriorate over time, it is safest to discard any stock that is more than 2 years old.
furtherInformation: It is, of course, essential to rinse containers thoroughly after cleaning them with bleaches. Bleaching powder, calcium hypochlorite, is an oxidising agent; cloths used with the powder might later ignite. Always rinse out such cloths thoroughly to remove traces of the powder. If bleach containing sodium hypochlorite is mixed with acids, the toxic gas chlorine will be released. Cleaning agents such as descalers and some lavatory cleaners contain acid but it may not always be possible to determine if other cleaners have acidic contents. Therefore, under no circumstances must bleach be mixed with, or used at the same time as, any other cleaning agent. Co-operation with cleaning staff over the methods to be used in food technology areas is essential.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Bleach is in the eyes
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Obtain medical attention. Irrigate immediately with water, holding eyelids apart and continue until the patient reaches hospital.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Chlorine is liberated
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Remove individual to fresh air and seek medical attention.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: and inhaled Bleach is swallowed
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Give plenty of water and seek medical attention. Do not induce vomiting. Bleach is spilt on the skin or Remove contaminated clothing. Wash affected area thoroughly with a large amount

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: clothes
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: of water. If a large area is affected or blistering occurs, seek medical attention. Soak contaminated clothing and rinse repeatedly.

sources.title: Cleaning agents for food handling areas: descalers
sources.process: The removal of scale from hard water from sinks, taps, toilet bowls, washbasins, baths, kettles and steam irons. All use some form of acid as the active ingredient.

hazards.label: Corrosive
hazards.detail: The acid component may be sodium hydrogensulfate or citric, formic, hydrochloric, phosphoric or sulfamic (aminosulfonic) acid. Those containing more than 10% formic acid, 25% hydrochloric acid, 25% phosphoric acid or 18% sodium hydrogensulfate are corrosive.

hazards.label: Irritant
hazards.detail: Descalers containing between 2 to 10% formic acid, 10 to 25% hydrochloric acid, 10 to 25% phosphoric acid, 6 to 18% sodium hydrogensulfate or sulfamic acid are irritant.

riskAssessment.label: Corrosive
riskAssessment.detail: The concentration of acid used varies considerably so that the level of risk in using different products is similarly variable. The ‘heavy duty’ formulations, classified as corrosive, are very hazardous, causing severe damage to the eyes and burns to the skin or alimentary canal, if swallowed.

riskAssessment.label: Irritant
riskAssessment.detail: The majority of descalers are more dilute but still irritant to the eyes or skin. At even lower concentrations of acid or if citric acid is the active ingredient, there may be no hazard warning on the product label but sensitive skin could be affected and eye contact gives discomfort.

controlMeasures: It is essential to wear gloves when using corrosive products. It is very strongly advised that the user wears a face shield when dispensing corrosive liquids and that these strong ones are avoided if this protection is not available. When using products which are powders, ensure that no dust is raised which could be inhaled or get into the eyes. When using irritant descalers, it is recommended that gloves are worn and that the eyes should be protected with safety spectacles.
restrictions: Descalers containing hydrochloric acid are not suitable for use with stainless steel surfaces. Pupils below year 12 must not be permitted to use descalers that are corrosive, though they may use less concentrated products, under supervision. Descalers must not be mixed with bleach because if a cleaner containing acid is mixed with bleach containing sodium (or calcium) hypochlorite, the toxic gas chlorine will be released. Therefore, under no circumstances must a descaler be mixed with, or used at the same time as, bleach or other cleaning agents.
disposal: Unwanted descaling liquids should be diluted by adding no more than 100 ml to a bucket of water before flushing down the foul-water drain. Alternatively, they can be neutralised by adding sodium carbonate (washing soda) until the fizzing stops, and then flushed away in any quantity. Empty containers may be added to ordinary waste.
storage: All descalers should be stored away from food areas and in a safe and secure place so that they cannot be taken by pupils without permission and misused.
furtherInformation: It is safest to use a descaling agent containing citric acid or one with the lowest concentration of acid compatible with the task to be performed. Cooperation with cleaning staff over the methods to be used in food technology areas is essential.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Descalers are in the eyes
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Wash thoroughly for at least ten minutes with water, holding the eyelids apart. Seek medical attention if irritation persists.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Descalers are swallowed
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Give plenty of water and seek medical attention. Do not induce vomiting.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Chlorine is liberated
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Remove patient to fresh air and seek medical attention.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Spilt on skin or clothes
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Remove contaminated clothing. Wash affected area thoroughly with a large amount of water. If a large area of skin is affected, seek medical attention. Soak contaminated clothing and rinse repeatedly.

sources.title: Cleaning agents for food handling areas: detergents
sources.process: Cleaning of hard surfaces, washing up pots, pans and cutlery by hand or with a machine.

hazards.label: Allergic reaction
hazards.detail: Some brands of detergents may contain enzymes and present the hazards of sensitisation and/or allergy.

hazards.label: Irritant
hazards.detail: Dishwasher chemicals often contain sodium silicate (metasilicate) and a bleaching agent such as sodium dichloroisocyanurate or sodium perborate; they may be very alkaline. Some hard-surface cleaners may contain sodium carbonate or 10 to 35% ammonia solution which also makes them alkaline. In such cases there is a serious hazard to the eyes.

riskAssessment.label: Allergic reaction
riskAssessment.detail: True allergic reactions to these detergent mixes are not common but, when they occur, they can be very troublesome to the sufferer.

riskAssessment.label: Irritant
riskAssessment.detail: All detergents, by their property of helping to dissolve grease, also remove natural oils from the skin leading to possible dryness, chafing and other dermatological problems, particularly in individuals with sensitive skin. The bleaching agents are also usually irritant.

controlMeasures: Where cleaning agents containing enzymes are used, protection with gloves is essential. When dispensing washing powders, avoid raising dust that might be inhaled or blow into the eyes. Although many detergent preparations are not classed as hazardous, it is strongly advised that all contact with the skin is avoided by wearing gloves, particularly for individuals who are recognised as having sensitive, damaged or dry skin. Where more aggressive cleaning agents marked ‘irritant’ are used, protection with gloves is essential. The eyes should be protected with safety spectacles when detergent preparations marked ‘irritant’ are handled.
restrictions: Although any preparation marked corrosive will normally be used only by adults or pupils below year 12 under close personal supervision, irritant cleaners could be used, with care, by younger pupils.
disposal: Cleaning agents used in food technology departments can be disposed of in the waste if solid or flushed down the foul-water drain if liquid.
storage: Detergents classed as ‘irritant’ and other cleaning materials should be stored in a safe place away from food areas.
furtherInformation: In the past, the detergents used in dishwashers have been strongly alkaline and rated corrosive. It appears that this is no longer true. The manufacturers have found alternative formulations that are just as effective at washing the pots and cutlery without the hazard.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Detergents are in the eyes
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Obtain medical attention. Irrigate immediately with water, holding the eyelids apart and continue irrigation until the casualty reaches hospital.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Swallowed
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Give plenty of water and seek medical attention. Do not induce vomiting.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Detergents likely to be
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Remove contaminated clothing. Wash affected area thoroughly with water. Apply a irritant contaminate the skin moisturising cream to affected skin. Soak contaminated clothing and rinse

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: or clothes
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: repeatedly.

sources.title: Cleaning agents for food handling areas: disinfectants
sources.process: The use of disinfectants to attempt to destroy microorganisms which may be present on surfaces etc in food technology areas.

hazards.label: Toxic
hazards.detail: Some industrial formulations of clear phenolic disinfectants are toxic.

hazards.label: Harmful
hazards.detail: Disinfectants containing some formulations of clear phenolics intended for domestic use are rated harmful.

hazards.label: Corrosive
hazards.detail: Certain phenolics, such as ‘Lysol’, are rated as corrosive and so is sodium hypochlorite when purchased at over 10% concentration.

hazards.label: Irritant
hazards.detail: Disinfectants containing sodium hypochlorite with between 5 to 10% active chlorine, sodium dichloroisocyanurate, ‘VirKon’ powder and some phenolics (including ‘Jeyes fluid’) are all rated irritant. Formulations containing between 0.2% and 1% formaldehyde (methanal) are also irritant.

riskAssessment.label: Toxic
riskAssessment.detail: No disinfectants labelled toxic are needed in food technology.

riskAssessment.label: Harmful
riskAssessment.detail: Concentrated disinfectants labelled harmful, present risks if they are swallowed.

riskAssessment.label: Corrosive
riskAssessment.detail: No disinfectants labelled corrosive are needed in food technology.

riskAssessment.label: Irritant
riskAssessment.detail: Some disinfectants labelled irritant (most are not) present risks to the skin and eyes. ‘VirKon’ powder and phenolics such as ‘Jeyes Fluid’ should also be kept off skin and away from the eyes and nose.

controlMeasures: Gloves and safety spectacles should be worn if concentrated, harmful disinfectants are handled. Handling phenolic disinfectants and preparing VirKon solutions also requires the use of gloves and safety spectacles.
restrictions: Pupils below year 12 must not be permitted to use disinfectants that are corrosive or toxic except under close personal supervision, though they may use disinfectants that are harmful or irritant.
disposal: Small quantities of disinfectants can be mixed with a bucket-full of water and flushed down the foul-water drain. Solids and empty containers can be added to other solid waste.
storage: All hazardous disinfectants should be stored away from food areas and in a safe place so that they cannot be handled by pupils without permission and misused.
furtherInformation: There are many different brands and types of disinfectant, varying considerably in their ability to destroy microorganisms. Chlorine-releasers Disinfectants with bleach (sodium hypochlorite) as the active ingredient, eg, ‘Domestos’; ‘Milton’, or sodium dichloroisocyanurate, eg, ‘Presept’, release chlorine in solution. These should be effective against a wide range of microorganisms (including viruses, if the strength is high enough) but are less suitable for very dirty conditions because they are degraded by organic matter; also they corrode metals. Bleach solution is recommended for all disinfection involving blood. Dilute hypochlorite solution is non-tainting and suitable for food preparation areas. Do not mix chlorine-releasing disinfectants with other cleaning agents. If the disinfectant in use is one containing sodium hypochlorite or dichloroisocyanurate and is mixed with acids, the toxic gas chlorine will be released. Therefore, under no circumstances must such disinfectants be mixed with, or used at the same time as, any other cleaning agent. Chloroxylenols These disinfectants, eg, ‘Dettol’, are not regarded as giving the best protection against a wide range of microorganisms and they are easily inactivated. They are, however, neither corrosive nor irritant. Diguanides Disinfectants which contain chlorhexidine, eg, ‘Hibitane’, or chlorhexidine mixed with the QAC cetrimide, eg, ‘Savlon’, are only really useful for skin disinfection. They should not be used for general disinfection tasks as they have limited activity. Formaldehyde Formaldehyde (methanal) is very effective in killing microorganisms but it is doubtful whether the concentrations used in cleaning agents is sufficient to do so quickly. Quaternary Ammonium Disinfectants with QACs as their active ingredient, eg, ‘Dettox’ or ‘Cetavlon’, have a Compounds (QACs) limited activity against microorganisms and are easily inactivated. They are not and appropriate for general disinfection tasks but are employed for cleaning equipment Ampholytic Surfactants and surfaces within the food and catering industries. Ampholytic surfactant disinfectants, such as ‘Tego’, have properties and limitations similar to QACs. Phenolics Clear phenolic disinfectants, eg, ‘Printol’, are active against bacteria and fungi but not viruses; unlike bleach, they are not readily broken down by organic matter, such as food remains or grease. They are unsuitable for use on any food preparation surface and are now difficult to obtain in sensible quantities. The use of other phenolic disinfectants is discouraged: black fluids or white fluids, eg, ‘Jeyes Fluid’, ‘Izal’ and especially ‘Lysol’ (because it is toxic and less effective than the others). ‘VirKon’ This powerful disinfectant is supplied as a powder and is effective against bacteria, fungi and viruses. The powder is rated irritant but, when made up as a 1% solution, is neither toxic nor irritant. The main active constituent is potassium peroxomonosufate, which works by oxidising the infective material. It should be used as the powder on blood spills.

sources.title: Cleaning agents for food handling areas: drain & sink cleaners
sources.process: The use of chemical cleaning agents to improve the flow through the drain from a sink and remove stains from the sink itself; many use strong acids or alkalis, others contain enzymes or hypochlorite.

hazards.label: Corrosive
hazards.detail: The majority of cleaners utilise caustic soda or potash (sodium or potassium hydroxide) as their active ingredient but some brands use sulfuric acid instead. (Many brands contain more than 50% active chemical; some even use pure sodium hydroxide pellets or undiluted acid.)

hazards.label: Allergic reaction
hazards.detail: Enzyme-based products may provoke a response in some people.

hazards.label: Irritant
hazards.detail: Products containing sodium hypochlorite with between 5 to 10% active chlorine or sodium dichloroisocyanurate are rated irritant.

hazards.label: Explosion
hazards.detail: Some cleaners contain a mix of sodium hydroxide and powdered aluminium that generates extremely flammable hydrogen gas.

riskAssessment.label: Corrosive
riskAssessment.detail: Brands are corrosive if the concentration is more than 2% sodium or potassium hydroxide or more than 15% sulfuric acid. They present high risks, causing severe damage to the eyes and burns to the skin or alimentary canal, if swallowed. Pellets or strong acid react with water making it hot enough to boil and cause splashes of corrosive chemical.

riskAssessment.label: Allergic reaction
riskAssessment.detail: Although much safer than the conventional caustic cleaners, there is a very small chance of an allergic response to the enzymes in these products. As it is impossible to identify in advance those individuals who may be hypersensitive, precautions should be observed.

riskAssessment.label: Irritant
riskAssessment.detail: Those products labelled irritant present risks to the skin and eyes.

riskAssessment.label: Explosion
riskAssessment.detail: Hydrogen-generating cleaners are used for clearing blocked drains and may present significant risks.

controlMeasures: Care must be taken to avoid splashes of liquid or raising dust when the corrosive cleaners are handled, protecting against inhalation or entry into the eyes. The skin must be protected by wearing suitable gloves1. A face shield must be used to protect the eyes when using pellets or liquid cleaners using more than 15% sulfuric acid. With dilute formulations, safety spectacles should be sufficient. The skin must be protected from any contact with enzymic cleaners by wearing gloves if there is any chance of an allergic reaction. When using sink or drain cleaners that are labelled irritant, safety spectacles should be worn if there is any risk of splashes to the eyes and gloves should be worn to protect the skin. All sources of ignition must be removed or extinguished when using cleaners that generate hydrogen.
Marigold Suregrip GO4Y or Blue Nitrile G25B are recommended. See CLEAPSS guidance leaflet PS 50, Gloves as personal Protective Equipment for a full discussion.
restrictions: Pupils must never be allowed to use corrosive sink cleaners. Any use to clear blockages must be the responsibility of staff who must read, and follow carefully, the instructions on the package.
disposal: Strong acids and alkalis may not be flushed directly into the drains except when using them for cleaning! Unwanted acid cleaners should be poured slowly into water (eg, a half bucket full for 200 ml of cleaner) while wearing a face shield, apron and gloves. Sodium carbonate (washing soda) can then be added until it stops fizzing. Strongly alkaline cleaners (sodium or potassium hydroxides or strong ammonia) are best disposed of with the help of the science department.
storage: All corrosive sink and drain cleaners should be stored away from food areas and in a safe and secure place so that they cannot be handled by pupils without permission and misused.

sources.title: Cleaning agents for food handling areas: oven cleaners
sources.process: Cleaning the insides of ovens using powders, liquids, gels, sprays and pads.

hazards.label: Corrosive
hazards.detail: Oven cleaners containing more than 2% sodium / potassium hydroxide are corrosive.

hazards.label: Irritant
hazards.detail: Oven cleaners containing between 0.5 to 2% sodium / potassium hydroxide are regarded as irritant.

hazards.label: Allergic reaction
hazards.detail: Enzyme-based products may provoke a response in some people.

riskAssessment.label: Corrosive
riskAssessment.detail: Oven cleaners are caustic; those that are most powerful contain high concentrations of (usually) sodium hydroxide and are corrosive. The cleaners may be applied as a thick gel (sometimes using a special applicator), with a pad or as a foam spray. The necessity of having to work in a confined area and reach into crevices and corners increases the risk of accidents during the use of such cleaners. Oven cleaners are easier to apply as a foam but may then be more readily sprayed onto exposed skin or into the eyes with potentially serious effects.

riskAssessment.label: Irritant
riskAssessment.detail: Formulations with lower concentrations of active ingredient are safer but nevertheless still irritant to skin and eyes.

riskAssessment.label: Allergic reaction
riskAssessment.detail: Although much safer than the conventional caustic cleaners, there is a very small chance of an allergic response to the enzymes in these products. As it is impossible to identify in advance those individuals who may be affected, precautions should be observed.

controlMeasures: Great care must be taken when using all corrosive oven cleaners, particularly those that are sprayed onto surfaces. The instructions supplied with the cleaners must be followed precisely. It is wise to apply the cleaning agent at arm’s length and to protect the skin from all contact with the cleaning agent and oven surfaces that have already been treated. The gloves should be long enough to cover the lower arm and the skin of the upper arm should not be exposed. The eyes must be adequately protected when using caustic cleaners. A face shield must be worn if there is a risk of corrosive materials being sprayed, splashed or wiped onto the face or into the eyes. The skin must be adequately protected from all contact with irritant cleaning agents. Gloves should be long enough to cover the lower arm and the skin of the upper arm should not be exposed. With agents that are marked irritant and with solid preparations, safety spectacles should provide sufficient eye protection. Gloves must be worn when using enzymic cleaners.
restrictions: Pupils below year 12 must not be permitted to use corrosive oven cleaners, though they may use less hazardous products under close supervision. It may be appropriate for older students to use oven cleaners that are corrosive but only if they are closely supervised and all the precautions listed above are followed. Spray or foam formulations, which are potentially more dangerous if misused, are not recommended for application by pupils.
disposal: Unwanted liquid cleaners can be mixed with a bucket-full of water and flushed down the foul-water drain. Other cleaners and empty containers can be added to other solid waste.
storage: All oven cleaners should be stored away from food areas and in a safe place so that they cannot be taken by pupils without permission and misused.
furtherInformation: If the oven cleaning operation produces an unpleasant smell, windows should be opened or extract fans used. Hazardous fumes are unlikely to be produced.

sources.title: Conventional ovens
sources.process: The use of a conventional oven for initial cooking and reheating of precooked food. See sheet 3.011 for the hazards of food poisoning and 3.023 for heating on hobs.

hazards.detail: Burning and scalding Cooking or reheating foods may result in a burn or scald to the skin.

hazards.label: Fire
hazards.detail: Overheated food, fats or cooking oil may ignite.

hazards.label: Explosion
hazards.detail: Gas that has not ignited presents a potential explosion hazard.

riskAssessment.detail: Burning and scalding Handling oven shelves and hot containers often result in minor burns and scalds. Cookers with controls at the back present an increased risk. The greatest risk occurs when putting items into, and removing them from, an oven particularly if hot shelves must be moved. When opening oven doors, blasts of hot, moist air / steam can cause involuntary movement and mist up spectacles.

riskAssessment.label: Fire
riskAssessment.detail: Oils and fats present the greatest risk of fire in the kitchen. Build up of debris in oven can cause fires.

riskAssessment.label: Explosion
riskAssessment.detail: Gas cookers should, if possible, be installed away from windows, otherwise sunlight can make flames invisible or draughts can blow out pilot lights and small flames.

controlMeasures: Correct instruction and appropriate use of oven gloves or cloths should minimise the risk of burns when putting dishes into or removing them from an oven. Oven gloves must always be used when putting items into, and removing them from, a hot oven. Oven shelves should be checked to see that they are in the required position, are level on their runners and cannot tip up when pulled out, laden with food. Care must be taken when opening oven doors, to guard against blasts of hot air. To reduce the dangers of accidents, the number of pupils working at any one time around heating equipment must be controlled. It is difficult to reduce the risk of fat-pan fires to zero so everyone must be taught how to deal safely with such a fire when it occurs. Open deep fat frying in not recommended in Food technology. The oven should be kept clean and free from build up of debris that could cause fires. Where siting is less than ideal, extra care must be taken to check pilot lights regularly or to confirm that gas has ignited properly.
restrictions: Food should not be heated or reheated while covered with certain plastic films; see sheet 3.019 for more information.
disposal: Cookers and other kitchen equipment should be disposed of in accordance with the Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment Regulations 2006 (the WEEE Regulations) See 3.034. Items should be taken to the local recycling point.
furtherInformation: If food covered with cling film is heated in an oven, it is important to ensure that the film is not touching the food. Care must be taken not to look too closely at roasting foods in case hot fat splashes into the eyes. Ensuring adequate heating of foods If cooking in a microwave oven then see sheet 3.027. If food is to be cooked at all, it is important to cook it thoroughly, following the correct conditions for each heating method and type of food and ensuring that the food is really very hot at the centre. It is safer to heat food during cooking or reheating until it is too hot and allow it to cool, rather than undercook or under-reheat food. If food is not piping hot throughout after cooking, bacteria causing gastroenteritis may still be present. It could be useful to check the settings on a conventional oven with a special oven thermometer from time to time. Where it is essential to keep cooked food hot for a period before it is consumed, see sheet 3.018. Dealing with fat-pan fires Although there are special fire extinguishers that are suitable for dealing with burning oil or fat, it is safest to use a fire blanket, damp towel or a tight-fitting lid to cut off the oxygen supply to the fire. This cover must stay in place until the pan is cold to prevent re-ignition. The use of water or the wrong extinguisher can seriously spread the fire with disastrous consequences.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Burns or scalds to the skin
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Cool the affected area under a running cold tap for ten minutes.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Serious burns to the skin
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Seek further medical assistance. Send for an ambulance. Cool the affected area under a running cold tap for ten minutes. Watch for difficulty in breathing or faintness. Gently remove jewellery or watches that might be difficult to remove later if the limb swells. Apply a dry dressing held in place by a cotton wool pad secured with a bandage or adhesive tape if the ambulance has not yet arrived.

immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Wash thoroughly for at least ten minutes with water to cool the eye as quickly as
