sources.title: Cooking and reheating, food poisoning
sources.process: The food poisoning hazards associated with use of any type of oven for initial cooking and reheating of precooked food. See sheet 3.010 for the burning and fire hazards.

hazards.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
hazards.detail: Gastrointestinal infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms (particularly E. coli 0157 and Salmonella) and/or their toxic products.

riskAssessment.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
riskAssessment.detail: While initial cooking destroys microorganisms and toxins, the temperature must be held sufficiently high for long enough to achieve this. Food chilled after cooking may become re-infected or remaining organisms may replicate (slowly) while chilled so that it must again reach a high temperature to ensure safety.

controlMeasures: Chicken and pork are the foods most likely to contain Salmonella while any meat could be contaminated with E. coli 0157 and cooking these foods thoroughly is essential. Pre-stuffed joints and poultry are sometimes difficult to heat throughout in a conventional oven and testing with a suitable, clean thermometer is advisable.
restrictions: Food should not be heated or reheated while covered with cling film; see sheet 3.019 for more information. Chilled food should not be left on tables or worktops before reheating: this allows the microorganisms to replicate and increases the risk that they will not be destroyed by the reheating process. Chilled food should go directly from the refrigerator to the oven. Cooked foods need to be cooled quickly, ideally using a blast chiller and then refrigerated.
furtherInformation: Ensuring adequate heating of foods If food is to be cooked at all, it is important to cook it thoroughly, following the correct conditions for each heating method and type of food and ensuring that the food is really very hot at the centre. If cooking in a microwave oven (see sheet 3.027), the conditions and standing times recommended by the manufacturer must be observed. To destroy bacteria during heating, food must reach an internal temperature of at least 70 °C for a minimum of 2 minutes. It is safer to heat food during cooking or reheating until it is too hot and allow it to cool, rather than undercook or under-reheat food. If food is not piping hot throughout after cooking, bacteria causing gastroenteritis may still be present. Food should normally be prepared just prior to serving; leaving perishable food out at room temperature for more than one hour or keeping food warm for extended periods should be avoided. Where it is essential to keep cooked food hot for a period before it is consumed, particular care over the temperature must be observed and regular checks of the temperature made. Reheating foods Liquid foods such as soups, stocks, sauces and gravy provide an ideal breeding ground for rapid microbial growth; such liquids can, however, be preserved by freezing after their preparation. If not frozen immediately, they should not be kept or reheated. Cooked food should be reheated only once, whether originally cooked in the home or purchased as a cook / chill product; any left-overs after reheating should be thrown away. Food should be reheated thoroughly, otherwise any bacteria that may have contaminated the food after the initial cooking or during storage can survive and reproduce. If bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus have multiplied in the food, they are capable of forming a heat-resistant toxin, so the food may still be unsafe even though it has been thoroughly heated. Cooked rice is particularly likely to contain spores of Bacillus cereus that have survived the cooking process.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Poisoning is suspected
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: If a casualty is suffering from nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea with drowsiness or unconsciousness, do not induce vomiting. Provided the casualty is conscious, wash out mouth with water. Obtain medical attention.

sources.title: Deep fat fryers
sources.process: Deep fat frying using a thermostatically controlled closed deep fat fryer.

hazards.label: Tripping and falling
hazards.detail: Trailing mains leads present a tripping hazard with a further hazard from the falling fryer.

hazards.label: Electric shock
hazards.detail: Electrically heated deep fat fryers present a hazard of electric shock.

hazards.label: Burns and Scalds
hazards.detail: Hot oil in contact with the skin may cause burns or scalds.

hazards.label: Overheating and Fire
hazards.detail: Hot oil is at risk of catching fire if heated to too high a temperature.

hazards.label: Environmental
hazards.detail: Used oil can cause environmental damage.

riskAssessment.label: Tripping and falling
riskAssessment.detail: The risk of tripping depends much more on the location of the socket outlets relative to the position of the deep fat fryer. This matter needs to be assessed locally. A falling fryer could cause a foot injury.

riskAssessment.label: Electric shock
riskAssessment.detail: The rate of wear and severity of the harm makes this a significant risk.

riskAssessment.label: Burns and Scalds
riskAssessment.detail: An increased risk when putting things into the fryer and the hand is likely to be closest. Removing hot items from the fryer could also present a risk.

controlMeasures: Frequent visual checks and regular formal inspections reduce the risk of electric shock. The fryer should be positioned in a dedicated area near to a socket outlet. Care should be taken that trailing leads are kept clear of work surfaces and people near by. Signs indicating ‘HOT’ would raise awareness to other classroom users. Instruction should be given on the correct use of deep fat fryers and adult supervision is advisable for pupils below Year 10. Only suitable ingredients and materials should be used in the deep fat fryer. Excess moisture should be removed from the ingredients before cooking. Fats and oils should be changed regularly. Attention needs to be paid to the correct disposal of used oil. Many local authorities have procedures to deal with this. It is difficult to reduce the risk of fat-pan fires to zero so everyone must be taught how to deal safely with such a fire when it occurs. Oven gloves should be used when handling hot food.
disposal: For disposal see 3.034.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Tripping and falling
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Wash thoroughly for at least ten minutes with water to prevent scratching of the eye. Seek medical attention if irritation persists.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Electric shocks
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Send for a first aider immediately. Taking care for your own safety, break contact by switching off or pulling out the plug. If it is necessary to move the casualty without switching off the supply, use a broom handle or wooden window pole or wear rubber gloves. If the casualty is unconscious and not breathing, check that the airways are clear and begin artificial ventilation. Send for an ambulance. If a trained first aider does not arrive quickly and the casualty has no pulse, consider carrying out cardio-pulmonary resuscitation.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Burns and scalds
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: If hot fat is splashed into the eyes: Wash thoroughly for at least ten minutes with water to cool the eye as quickly as possible. Seek medical attention if irritation persists. If burns to the skin occur: Cool the affected area under a running cold tap for ten minutes. If serious burns to the skin occur: Send for an ambulance. Cool the affected area under a running cold tap for ten minutes. Watch for difficulty in breathing or faintness. Gently remove jewellery or watches that might be difficult to remove later if the limb swells. Apply a dry dressing held in place by a cotton wool pad secured with a bandage or adhesive tape if the ambulance has not yet arrived.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Fire
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Although there are special fire extinguishers that are suitable for dealing with burning oil or fat, it is safest to use a fire blanket, damp towel or a tight-fitting lid to cut off the oxygen supply to the fire. This cover must stay in place until the pan is cold to prevent re-ignition. The use of water or the wrong extinguisher can seriously spread the fire with disastrous consequences.

sources.title: Defrosting foods
sources.process: Defrosting foods that are precooked and defrosting food that is to be cooked.

hazards.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
hazards.detail: Gastrointestinal infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxic products.

riskAssessment.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
riskAssessment.detail: Freezing does not kill the organisms causing food poisoning, it stops them from multiplying rapidly. There is a negligible risk with precooked food which is eaten cold (eg, a frozen cake). Frozen meat, particularly poultry, may not reach a temperature high enough to kill Campylobacter or Salmonella during cooking if cooked from frozen. The cooking can then encourage the growth of pathogenic microorganisms in parts of the food.

controlMeasures: It is essential to follow the supplier’s instructions that are printed on frozen poultry. Should there be no instructions, the bird should be thawed thoroughly by leaving at room temperature for up to 8 hours. Other meat is usually defrosted by leaving it overnight in a refrigerator. Prepared dishes are often cooked from frozen but those that have been frozen in a domestic freezer are best defrosted before reheating.
restrictions: Food that has become defrosted as a result of a power or freezer failure should be disposed of and not eaten.
disposal: Any frozen food that is discovered to be well-past its ‘best-before date’ should be placed in the solid waste.
storage: Commercially frozen food is given a ‘star rating’ to indicate how long it should be stored in a freezer: 1 week 1 month until ‘best-before date’.
furtherInformation: When shopping, it is best to select chilled and frozen foods last to minimise the amount of time during which the food can warm up in transit. If possible, also avoid purchasing such foods at times when queues could build up at the check-out. Pack frozen and chilled foods in separate bags and, wherever possible, use an insulated food bag for transporting such items home to avoid any significant temperature increase. All chilled and frozen foods must be placed immediately into a well maintained refrigerator or freezer. It is essential to read and follow thawing instructions on frozen foods thoroughly and carefully. This will not only be safer but also restores the best flavour and texture. Items should be placed on a tray, plate or dish that is sufficiently deep to collect any liquid that drips from the thawed product. Overloading the dish with several frozen items should be avoided because this prolongs the thawing time and results in the food on the outside of the dish thawing first. While the food is thawing, it should be covered to prevent contamination from the atmosphere and kept in a cool place; although this takes longer, the food will thaw more thoroughly and will be safer. If defrosting is to be done in a microwave oven, see sheet 3.027. Thawing times depend on the thickness and mass of foods and many small items, such as fish fillets, burgers and vegetables, may be cooked straight from the frozen state. Thawed food should not be refrozen unless cooked thoroughly.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Poisoning is suspected
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: If a casualty is suffering from nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea with drowsiness or unconsciousness, do not induce vomiting. Provided the casualty is conscious, wash out mouth with water. Obtain medical attention.

sources.title: Eating and tasting
sources.process: Tasting during preparation (for flavour adjustment) and consuming food after preparation and cooking as the end point of the activity. Sensory analysis activities.

hazards.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
hazards.detail: Gastrointestinal infection results from eating or hand-to-mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxic products.

hazards.label: Poisons on food
hazards.detail: Poisoning which is not an infection results from eating or hand-to-mouth contact with, food containing natural toxic chemicals or contaminants from the environment.

hazards.label: Food contamination
hazards.detail: Food may become contaminated during or after preparation by someone carrying an infectious disease.

hazards.label: Allergic reaction
hazards.detail: Allergic reactions may develop from exposure to many foods. Some people have become ‘sensitised’, ie, even a very small dose of the allergen then produces the reaction. Substances likely to cause reactions include peanuts, milk, flour (gluten) and food additives.

riskAssessment.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
riskAssessment.detail: Even fresh food of the highest quality should be expected to be carrying organisms that will lead to decay. One purpose of cooking food is to control this process but, if food is not sufficiently fresh when purchased, cooking it may be too late to prevent problems. Careless handling within the kitchen may also lead to contamination, in particular, storing food inappropriately.

riskAssessment.label: Poisons on food
riskAssessment.detail: Foods are frequently contaminated with pesticides, fungicides or fertilisers during their production. Even foods that are produced by ‘organic’ methods are not necessarily free of natural poisons.

riskAssessment.label: Food contamination
riskAssessment.detail: Tasting food with a dirty spoon may be a source of infection. Similarly, when food is tasted by a group of pupils, shared spoons, forks and dishes may lead to the transmission of microorganisms.

riskAssessment.label: Allergic reaction
riskAssessment.detail: Any ‘foreign’ protein may produce an allergic response in sensitive individuals and inadvertent consumption of traces of nuts have been known to cause anaphylactic shock.

controlMeasures: The highest standards of hygiene must be maintained at all times and particularly when pupils are working closely together in the same area. (See Food Safety Regulations in the Introduction to Part 3.) The normal methods of preparation of food are designed to minimise any harmful effects that result from contaminants on the surface. When tasting food while cooking, a clean utensil must be used by each individual with immediate washing. If further tasting is necessary, another clean utensil must be used, again washing it as soon as tasting is completed. For group tasting sessions, it is sensible to provide a collection of disposable materials, such as paper plates and cups together with plastic spoons, etc. Allergic reactions can only be controlled by awareness of problems and separation of sufferers from their allergens.
restrictions: ‘At risk’ groups should avoid some foods altogether or eat them with caution. Everyone is potentially at risk from the effects of food poisoning but certain groups are more susceptible than others. These include: • children under 2-years old; • pregnant women; • elderly people; • people taking drugs which suppress the body’s natural ability to fight infection; • individuals on extensive treatment with antibiotics or receiving chemotherapy; • people with reduced immunity, including AIDS sufferers, alcoholics, drug abusers, diabetics, transplant patients, those who are already ill or convalescent and those with known allergies.

Foods that ‘at risk’ groups should avoid Foods that are safe for ‘at risk’ groups Foods potentially contaminated with Listeria cytogenes, eg, Pasteurised, sterilised or UHT milk; hard cheese such as raw, unpasteurised milk and its products, soft cheese such as Cheshire, Cheddar and Lancashire; processed soft cheese, Brie, Camembert or blue-veined types, and soft-whip ice including cream cheese and cheese spreads, fromage frais, cream from vendors’ machines. fetta, cottage cheese; yoghurt; block ice-cream. Pâté: meat, fish or vegetable (unless in a jar or can), Jars or cans of pâté but stored in fridge and consumed within particularly from a delicatessen. 2 days of opening. Raw or undercooked meat; precooked or ready-roasted Fermented and dehydrated meat products, eg, salami. poultry. Raw eggs or dishes prepared with raw, unpasteurised eggs, Commercially-prepared egg dishes using pasteurised eggs; eg, mayonnaise, egg custard, egg nog, Hollandaise sauce, UHT, frozen or dried eggs and their products; well-cooked egg soufflés, mousses, Royal icing; lightly-cooked eggs or dishes dishes. made from eggs cooked in this way.
furtherInformation: An unpleasant smell, unusual texture or tainted flavour may indicate the presence of large numbers of microbes in food. Pathogens and microorganisms producing toxins may also be present even if food does not appear to be contaminated. With sufficient time, nutrients, moisture and a suitable temperature, bacteria and other microorganisms will replicate rapidly. (A bacterium reproducing every 20 minutes will produce a colony containing 16,777,216 cells within 8 hours. Less than 1 million bacteria are sufficient to cause food poisoning in some cases.) The symptoms of food poisoning vary according to the microorganism involved but may include nausea, headache, aching joints, vomiting and diarrhoea. Symptoms may develop rapidly or after an incubation period. If this delay is longer than 2 days, it is difficult to trace the poisoning incident to the food responsible. (See Appendix 3 for an illustration of the major causes of food poisoning.) If charges are made for food, it will be necessary to comply with the various food safety regulations, eg, to ensure that hair is covered etc. Charging for refreshments may also lead to inspection.

immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: If a casualty is suffering from nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea with drowsiness or unconsciousness, do not induce vomiting. Provided the casualty is conscious, wash out mouth with water. Obtain medical attention.

sources.title: Enzymes
sources.process: Enzymes may be used in making cheese and junket, to tenderise meat, in extracting juice from fruit purées and for a variety of other tasks.

hazards.label: Allergic reaction
hazards.detail: Allergic reactions may develop from exposure to culinary enzymes used in preparing foods. Some people have become ‘sensitised’, ie, even a very small dose of the allergen then produces the reaction. Substances likely to cause sensitisation are identified by risk phrases R42 (May cause sensitisation by inhalation) & R43 (May cause sensitisation by skin contact).

riskAssessment.label: Allergic reaction
riskAssessment.detail: Enzymes are proteins and any ‘foreign’ protein may produce an allergic response in sensitive individuals. An individual may initially become sensitised to the enzyme so that the briefest subsequent exposure will trigger an allergic response. In food technology, a significant exposure to enzymes will be extremely unlikely and they therefore present little, if any, risk for most individuals. It is those making up the enzyme solution who are most at risk because of the possibility of inhaling the powdered enzyme. It is, however, impossible to predict or identify in advance those who might be affected when handling the enzymes, so precautions should be taken by all.

controlMeasures: When enzyme solutions are being prepared from powders, it is important to avoid creating and inhaling any dust. If dust is likely to be inhaled, a dust mask (type FFP31) should be worn. Any direct contact between enzyme powders or strong solutions and the skin should also be avoided, so protective gloves2 should be worn. Specialist advice and support should be sought (eg, from Science teachers or technicians)
The new European Standard for ‘disposable particulate respirators’ is EN 149:2001. The older type number was FFP3S. See CLEAPSS leaflet PS 50, Gloves as Personal Protective Equipment.
restrictions: Persons with known allergic reactions to enzymes should be particularly careful to take appropriate control measures because of the risk of anaphylactic shock.
disposal: Any unwanted stocks of enzymes should be mixed with a lot of water and flushed into the foul-water drain.
storage: Enzyme solutions should not be stored for more than a few weeks since they work better when fresh but, if it is necessary, they should be kept cool.
furtherInformation: There should be no risks involved in consuming the enzymes naturally contained in food.

immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Immediately wash the eye thoroughly for at least ten minutes with water. Seek

sources.title: Food processors
sources.process: Using food processors that are not held in the hand during use.

hazards.label: Cuts
hazards.detail: The sharp blades may give rise to cuts.

hazards.label: Electric shock
hazards.detail: Damage to the casing of the processor or to the power cord can present an electric shock hazard. Water inside the motor or control sections could defeat the electrical insulation.

hazards.label: Manual handling
hazards.detail: Some machines are heavy and present a manual handling hazard.

riskAssessment.label: Cuts
riskAssessment.detail: The blades are very sharp and can cause cuts even when not rotating. If they are accessible when the processor is running they present a high risk.

riskAssessment.label: Electric shock
riskAssessment.detail: Risks may arise from damaged and incorrectly wired plugs, the fitting in the plug of a fuse with an inappropriate rating for the equipment and flexible cables which have been damaged or allowed to become worn, impairing the insulation. The risk of shock from water inside the electrical section is probably small but still significant.

riskAssessment.label: Manual handling
riskAssessment.detail: Lifting a heavy machine from a low cupboard or carrying it between rooms present a risk of injury to the back or arms.

controlMeasures: Manufacturer’s instructions should be followed at all times. Instruction should be given on the use of machines. All processors should be fitted with an interlock to prevent operation unless guarded against insertion of fingers. The correct functioning of this interlock should be confirmed regularly. Users must be trained to isolate the machine from the power supply before dismantling it for cleaning. Clear instructions for dismantling and cleaning must be available. Blades should be stored appropriately. Frequent visual checks and regular formal inspections reduce the risk of electric shock from faults to a low level. Cleaning methods must not allow water inside the electrical parts. Users must be trained to move heavy machines correctly, using two persons if necessary. Any movements between rooms or buildings should have an individual risk assessment to identify a safe method and route.
restrictions: Although food processors are very safe to use, some classes may contain pupils who are too disruptive to be trusted with expensive equipment.
disposal: See 3.034. The Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment Regulations 2006 (the WEEE Regulations) apply.
storage: Heavy food processors should not be stored on shelves that are very high or very low, nor on shelves incapable of supporting the weight.
furtherInformation: An electrical safety inspection and test may miss a mechanical interlock which prevents the processor being used unless it is correctly assembled with covers or lids in place. It is therefore strongly recommended that a regular inspection is used to confirm that the safety system is working correctly. If the processor is used irregularly, an inspection before each use may be more practicable.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Cuts
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: If cuts are minor, ie, of a sort which casualties would normally treat themselves, the wound should be washed clean and a small, sterilised dressing applied.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Severe cuts
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Send for a first aider. Apply pressure on or as close to the cut as possible, using fingers or a pad of cloth. Leave any embedded large bodies and press round them. Lower the casualty to the floor and raise the wound as high as possible. Protect yourself from contamination by blood. Blood splashes or drips should be cleaned up with VirKon as on sheet 3.007.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Electric shock
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Send for a first aider immediately. Taking care for your own safety, break contact by switching off or pulling out the plug. If it is necessary to move the casualty without switching off the supply, use a broom handle or wooden window pole or wear rubber gloves. If the casualty is unconscious and not breathing, check that the airways are clear and begin artificial ventilation. Send for an ambulance. If a trained first aider does not arrive quickly and the casualty has no pulse, consider carrying out cardio-pulmonary resuscitation.

sources.title: Food storage: dry foods
sources.process: Storage of dry food items such as flour, sugar, pulses, rice and canned foods.

hazards.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
hazards.detail: Gastrointestinal infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxic products.

hazards.label: Poisons on food
hazards.detail: Poisoning which is not an infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food containing natural toxic chemicals or contaminants from their environment.

riskAssessment.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
riskAssessment.detail: Bacteria will not multiply in dry foods but they can be introduced by pests and multiply during food preparation. They should not be present in intact cans or other food containers but may enter if the container has been accidentally damaged or once it has been opened. The longer food is kept, the more likely it is to become infested.

riskAssessment.label: Poisons on food
riskAssessment.detail: The risks of food becoming contaminated by transfer from other foods or from their environment are greater in storage without adequate segregation. If dry foods are stored with cleaning agents or equipment, the risk of contamination is significant.

controlMeasures: The storage cupboard should be designed to minimise the problem. Shelves should be cleaned and tidied on a regular basis with stock rotated so that the oldest items are always used first. All food should be kept labelled and covered; opened packs should be placed in airtight containers. Staff should be vigilant for signs of pests. Cans should be inspected for rust, dents or ‘blown’ ends; if there is reason to be suspicious, their contents should not be eaten. Proper segregation in storage necessary to prevent contamination.
storage: Use by dates should be observed. Dry foods stored in airtight containers will keep for a long time but should be inspected before use (for weevils or mould) and pulses may need longer cooking times than fresh ones. Cans should keep, unopened, for up to 3 years. Once they have been opened, and if their contents will not all be used at once, the food should be emptied into a non- metallic container, covered and refrigerated.
furtherInformation: The store cupboard for dry foodstuffs should be: • cool, dry, well-ventilated and, if appropriate, well-lit; • designed so that pests have no way of entering; • such that all food can be stored above floor level; • ideally of such a size that similar foods can be placed together with space for an unopened container behind the one in use; • not used for storage of anything else. It is important to use up stock in rotation so that the oldest is used first.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Poisoning is suspected
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: If a casualty is suffering from nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea with drowsiness or unconsciousness, do not induce vomiting. Provided the casualty is conscious, wash out mouth with water. Obtain medical attention.

sources.title: Food storage: high temperatures
sources.process: Keeping cooked food warm until it is to be consumed.

hazards.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
hazards.detail: Gastrointestinal infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxic products.

riskAssessment.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
riskAssessment.detail: Food that is to be eaten hot, but cannot be consumed immediately, may harbour microorganisms which multiply during the period between cooking and eating when the food is still warm.

controlMeasures: It is essential to store the food in such a way that its temperature is raised above 63 °C throughout the period between cooking and consumption. Steps must be taken to ensure that the heat supply is such that all of the food is maintained at the required temperature. Regular temperature checks with a food probe should be made.
restrictions: If a suitable thermometer is not available to demonstrate that this temperature is being achieved, no attempt should be made to keep food hot in this way.
furtherInformation: It is always recommended that food should be consumed immediately after cooking. If this is impossible for some reason, it is preferable to cool the food quickly, ideally using a blast chiller, store it in a refrigerator and then reheat thoroughly later. Advice should be given to pupils on the reheating of dishes prepared in school and then taken home. It is unusual for in food technology in schools and colleges to need to keep cooked food hot. However, it is necessary for special projects or occasions when visitors are involved.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Poisoning is suspected
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: If a casualty is suffering from nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea with drowsiness or unconsciousness, do not induce vomiting. Provided the casualty is conscious, wash out mouth with water. Obtain medical attention.

sources.title: Food storage: low temperatures
sources.process: Preserving the quality of food by chilling and freezing.

hazards.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
hazards.detail: Gastrointestinal infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxic products.

hazards.label: Poisons on food
hazards.detail: Contamination of fatty foods wrapped in plastic films with chemicals from the plastic.

riskAssessment.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
riskAssessment.detail: Harmful bacteria require food, moisture, warmth and time to survive and multiply. All reproduce rapidly at temperatures around 37 °C (ie, body temperature), but many can multiply at lower or higher temperatures. Some can do so, although slowly, at temperatures even as low as 5 °C. Some foods are a greater risk than others (see below). Neglect of temperature control may have been the cause of a majority of food poisoning cases in recent years.

riskAssessment.label: Poisons on food
riskAssessment.detail: Problems that were identified in the 1970s with PVC-based films have largely been eliminated by changing the formulation of the plastic used. Nevertheless, fatty foods are more likely than others to absorb any chemicals released by plastic packaging. Even in the worst cases, the concentration of such contaminants is likely to be very low and so present no problem.

controlMeasures: A refrigerator that stores food at a temperature below 5 °C can delay bacterial growth for up to 5 days. Those foods that are listed below should be kept in such a refrigerator for even short-term storage. See Further Information for Good practice in safe refrigerator management. For long-term storage, food should be kept at -18 °C. Although bacteria will survive at this temperature, they will not be able to multiply until the temperature is raised. See Further Information for Good practice in safe freezer management. Although film made from polyethylene or from VDC copolymer plastics, eg, ‘microwave and freezer wrap’, is safer, the advice of the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food was that it is unwise to distinguish between different types of food wrap. There is no evidence of a health hazard from any type of cling film but little is known of the chemicals that migrate from the plastics into food and so it is sensible to minimise the contact between fatty foods and films.
disposal: Frozen or chilled foods past their use-by dates must be disposed of (see 3.034).
furtherInformation: Those foods that are a greater risk and therefore need more care include the following. • All meat and poultry products which may be contaminated with food poisoning bacteria. • Raw fish and shellfish are especially likely to harbour bacteria able to multiply at low temperatures and may have come from polluted waters. • Milk, eggs and foods containing them such as cream, custard or mayonnaise that provide an ideal mixture of nutrients needed by multiplying bacteria. • Cooked meat and gravy, soups and stock which are also ideal media for bacteria. • Cooked rice is likely to contain bacterial spores that have survived the cooking process. If such foods are not cool enough, a small number of bacteria can become millions very quickly. Good practice in safe refrigerator management 1 Keep the refrigerator door tightly closed, open only when necessary and close it promptly. 2 Keep the refrigerator clean and free from any build-up of ice. 3 Remove old items once use by date has been reached. 4 Fit a thermometer, which can be seen easily and checked daily, on the inside wall or wire shelf 15 cm from the outside edge and half way down the refrigerator. Temperatures should be between 1 and 4 °C. (There will be a variation of 2 or 3 degrees between different parts of the refrigerator.) 5 Allow cold air to circulate; do not overfill the refrigerator. 6 Follow storage instructions and observe ‘eat-by’ dates on labels. 7 Keep all food covered. 8 Food should be cool before being put into the refrigerator, eg, do not use it to set jelly quickly. 9 Raw food and cooked food must be kept entirely separate to avoid cross-contamination. 10 Raw meat and poultry should be isolated and placed where juices cannot drip onto other food. 11 Fresh fruit and vegetables should be washed before storage in a salad crisper drawer. 12 Food to be stored should be clearly labelled with contents, date of storage and use-by date. Good practice in safe freezer management 1 Frozen food deteriorates in flavour and texture with time. How long it should be stored depends on the type of food and the rating of the freezer, usually from 3 months to 1 year. 2 Keep the door or lid tightly closed, open only when necessary and close it promptly. 3 Keep the freezer clean and free from any build-up of ice. 4 Defrost regularly and dispose of any out of date items. 5 Display a freezer thermometer where it can be seen so the reading checked easily (-18 °C). 6 Wrap food adequately (see below), seal, label and date so that it can be used in rotation. 7 Display and follow manufacturers’ instructions on storage times and temperatures. 8 Never refreeze food that has been thawed. Wrapping foods for storage in refrigerators and freezers Do not use cling film to wrap fatty foods (eg, cheese, butter, cooked meats or cakes / biscuits with chocolate or cream coatings, etc). Either place the food in containers which are then covered with cling film so that it is not in contact with the food or use sealable containers, plastic bags or aluminium foil instead. Cling film can be used to wrap non-fatty foods such as most fruit and vegetables.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Poisoning is suspected
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: If a casualty is suffering from nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea with drowsiness or unconsciousness, do not induce vomiting. Provided the casualty is conscious, wash out mouth with water. Obtain medical attention.

sources.title: Freezing food: freezer, refrigerator
sources.process: The use of domestic-type freezers and refrigerators for freezing raw and cooked foods.

hazards.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
hazards.detail: Gastrointestinal infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxic products.

riskAssessment.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
riskAssessment.detail: Harmful bacteria require food, moisture, warmth and time to survive and multiply. All reproduce rapidly at temperatures around 37 °C (ie, body temperature), but many can multiply at lower or higher temperatures. If food is not frozen through to the centre, the bacteria can continue to multiply so that when the food is de-frosted and consumed infection can result. If the food to be frozen is above room temperature when placed in the freezer, it may cause local thawing of other foods before the cooling system extracts the heat. This may allow bacteria to multiply in the neighbouring items.

controlMeasures: Food to be frozen must be placed in the coldest part of a domestic refrigerator or freezer with any controls also set to achieve the lowest possible temperature. Food to be frozen must already be close to room temperature before being frozen. Food to be frozen should be labeled clearly with contents and date.
restrictions: Cook / chill foods must not be kept, even in a refrigerator at a temperature below 5 °C, after the ‘use-by’ date. They must also be discarded if the temperature of the refrigerator rises above 5 °C. Similarly, any frozen food should be discarded (or used immediately) if the freezer temperature rises above the temperature indicated by the ‘star rating’ of the food. (See 3.013.)
furtherInformation: Food which is preserved by freezing must not only be safe (ie, not containing significant quantities of harmful bacteria or their toxic products) but must also be nutritious while maintaining an acceptable texture and flavour. This can be achieved if the food is of high quality initially, is properly prepared and frozen quickly (to ensure that the ice forms small crystals). Natural enzymes in the food remain active at chilling temperatures around 8 °C. This can be useful in tenderising meat but, in vegetables and fruit, it causes loss of vitamin C and carotene. The preparation therefore depends on the foodstuff as below. • Fish tenderises rapidly and is frozen within hours of being caught. • Poultry is chilled overnight and then frozen quickly. • Veal and pork are chilled for two or three days before being frozen. • Beef and lamb are chilled for about a week before freezing. • Vegetables are blanched (but not cooked) to destroy the enzymes, cooled with iced water and then frozen quickly. • Fruit is washed and frozen in sugar solution. Commercial freezing methods Because of the advantages of freezing foods quickly, commercial freezers use several different techniques to achieve this. • Plate freezing - the oldest method, where the food in containers is gently pressed onto very cold plates. • Air-blast freezing - very commonly used, where the food is placed on trays and passed under a blast of very cold air. • Immersion freezing - used for large items (eg, turkeys), where the food is immersed in a freezing solution (salt water, sugar solution or polyethylene glycol). Once frozen, the food is centrifuged to remove the remaining solution. • Spray freezing - used for delicate or high-cost items, where the food is sprayed with liquid nitrogen or liquid carbon dioxide to achieve very rapid cooling. • Flow freezing - used for vegetables and berries, where the food is supported on a cushion of cold air (a fluidised bed) as it passes through a freezer chamber. Cook / chill foods Cook / chill foods cannot be prepared using a conventional refrigerator or freezer; once chilled using a blast-chiller, they must be kept in a refrigerator at a temperature below 5 °C. They may be stored for up to 5 days after preparation. If they are not eaten by then they must be discarded. They must also be discarded if the temperature of the refrigerator rises above 5 °C. Cook / chill foods should be heated immediately before being eaten, to at least 75 °C, for 10 to 30 minutes, depending on the size of the portion. Keeping food after a lesson In many educational establishments, classes will not be able to consume food immediately it has been prepared but will want to take it home at the end of the day. Arrangements should ideally be made to keep this food covered and cool until the individual pupil or student can collect it.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Poisoning is suspected
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: If a casualty is suffering from nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea with drowsiness or unconsciousness, do not induce vomiting. Provided the casualty is conscious, wash out mouth with water. Obtain medical attention.

sources.title: Frying and grilling food
sources.process: The use of a frying pan for shallow frying and a powered deep-fat fryer with or without a lid. The use of a gas- or electrically-heated grill.

hazards.label: Fire
hazards.detail: Oil and fat, when heated to a sufficiently high temperature, produce vapours that ignite easily.

hazards.label: Burns
hazards.detail: Hot oil, flames, hotplates and elements, together with hot pans and lids, all present a burn hazard.

hazards.label: Eye damage
hazards.detail: The eye may be damaged by splashes or spitting of hot fat or oil.

riskAssessment.label: Fire
riskAssessment.detail: The risk of fire is greatest when using a pan of deep fat on a hob. The consequent risk of injury is greatest in busy areas with several students working together around one appliance. Open deep fat frying is not recommended. Oil in a wok is easily ignited but is not serious if there is only a little in use.

riskAssessment.label: Burns
riskAssessment.detail: Sunlight can make flames invisible. An increased risk occurs when putting items into a fryer and the hand is likely to be closest. Removing a hot and heavy pan from a hob to a worktop may also present a high risk.

riskAssessment.label: Eye damage
riskAssessment.detail: The risk is greatest when turning food during frying or when adding items to a pan of hot fat or oil.

controlMeasures: To reduce the dangers of accidents, the number of pupils working at any one time around heating equipment must be controlled. All persons must be trained to deal correctly with a fat or oil fire. Woks should not be left unattended during heating. Gas cookers and hobs should, if possible, be installed away from windows, to improve the visibility of flames and reduce the effects of draughts on pilot lights and small flames. It may be necessary to use oven gloves when moving a hot fryer or its lid. It is necessary to check that rings above gas burners are firmly in place before starting to use a hob. Although one would not normally use eye protection in a domestic kitchen, in a place of work such as a food technology department, protective spectacles should be worn to control the risk to the eyes.
restrictions: Pupils who are not sufficiently mature (typically below year 12) should not use chip pans on hobs.
disposal: For disposal see 3.034.
furtherInformation: Dealing with fat-pan fires Although there are special fire extinguishers that are suitable for dealing with burning oil or fat, it is safest to use a fire blanket, damp towel or a tight-fitting lid to cut off the oxygen supply to the fire. This cover must stay in place until the pan is cold to prevent re-ignition. The use of water or the wrong extinguisher can seriously spread the fire with disastrous consequences.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Hot fat is splashed
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Wash thoroughly for at least ten minutes with water to cool the eye as quickly as

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: into the eyes
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: possible. Seek medical attention if irritation persists.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Burns to the skin
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Cool the affected area under a running cold tap for ten minutes.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Serious burns to the skin
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Send for an ambulance. Cool the affected area under a running cold tap for ten minutes. Watch for difficulty in breathing or faintness. Gently remove jewellery or watches that might be difficult to remove later if the limb swells. Apply a dry dressing held in place by a cotton wool pad secured with a bandage or adhesive tape if the ambulance has not yet arrived.

sources.title: Handling food
sources.process: Handling all food substances and products.

hazards.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
hazards.detail: Eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxic products may result in gastro-intestinal infection.

hazards.label: Poisons on food
hazards.detail: Poisoning which is not an infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food containing natural toxic chemicals or contaminants from the environment.

hazards.label: Allergic reaction
hazards.detail: Allergic reactions may develop from exposure to many foods. Some people have become ‘sensitised’, ie, even a very small dose of the allergen then produces the reaction. Substances likely to cause reactions include peanuts, milk, flour (gluten) and food additives.

riskAssessment.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
riskAssessment.detail: If high standards of hygiene are not maintained while preparing food, pathogenic microorganisms may be transferred to the food from the handler or from other foods via the work surface or utensils as well as from other foods directly.

riskAssessment.label: Poisons on food
riskAssessment.detail: Carelessness or ignorance of the appropriate preparation techniques increases the risk of natural toxins being consumed but items presenting risks are restricted to red kidney beans, green or sprouting parts of potatoes and rhubarb leaves. Chemical residues, eg, from pesticides, may also be present but rarely at significant concentrations.

riskAssessment.label: Allergic reaction
riskAssessment.detail: Any ‘foreign’ protein may produce an allergic response in sensitive individuals but simply handling the offending substance is unlikely to produce anything worse than skin irritation. However, inadvertent consumption of traces of nuts have caused anaphylactic shock.

controlMeasures: Strict adherence to the highest standards of personal hygiene is required (see the Introduction to Part 3). Every effort must be made to ensure clean working conditions (see 3.003) and to avoid contamination from other foods via utensils (see also 3.011 & 3.024). Washing is adequate to remove chemical residues from most fruit and vegetables. The treatment for natural toxins depends on the food. Rhubarb stalks should have all the leaves removed before cooking as should green and sprouting parts of potatoes. Red kidney beans must be cooked as thoroughly as during the canning process. Allergic reactions can only be controlled by awareness of problems and separation of sufferers from their allergens.
restrictions: Persons suffering from sickness, diarrhoea, colds, coughs or other infections should not prepare food for consumption by others.
furtherInformation: International food safety requirements Under the auspices of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, the Codex Alimentarius Commission has created a series of guidelines, standards and other recommendations to ensure food hygiene internationally. These include a Recommended International Code of Practice - General Principles of Food Hygiene that uses a Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) system for its application. If this system is followed, the foodstuffs that now travel from all parts of the world to our shops will meet common standards for safety, wholesomeness and safe levels of chemical contaminants. Preventing contamination of food after purchase Avoid putting cooked or ready-to-eat foods on to a surface that has just had raw food prepared on it. Raw food, especially meat and fish, is more likely to have bacteria on it than cooked food. Cheese should therefore not come into direct contact with meat or surfaces where meat has been prepared. Raw and cooked foods should be kept separate and where possible and appropriate, covered or wrapped. Avoid adding freshly-prepared food to items prepared previously or putting freshly-prepared food into unwashed containers. Wash poultry, fish and offal thoroughly in clean, cold, running water. Keep these items cool and covered in between preparation processes, so far as possible. Wash fruit, vegetables and salads in clean, cold, running water and keep cool in clean, covered containers until required. Throw away old food wrappings such as foil, cling film or polythene bags and use fresh, clean, food wrappings. Do not wrap fatty foods with cling film; chemicals may leach out of the film into the food. (See 3.019 for more information.) Look out for the appearance of insect pests, particularly in food cupboards, and deal with infestations before they build up; animals carry bacteria that can contaminate food preparation areas and work surfaces. Students should be advised to keep pet animals at home out of the kitchen and away from food storage and preparation areas. Change and wash tea towels and dish cloths daily, otherwise bacteria can build up and contaminate any surface with which the cloths come into contact. Students should be advised to exercise special care and caution after handling domestic washing at home. Soiled washing can spread bacteria, especially if a family member has an infection or diarrhoea. They should be instructed never to sort out soiled washing on surfaces where food is prepared and always to wash hands after handling soiled washing.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Poisoning is suspected
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: If a casualty is suffering from nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea with drowsiness or unconsciousness, do not induce vomiting. Provided the casualty is conscious, wash out mouth with water. Obtain medical attention.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Anaphylactic shock
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: If the patient suffers from impaired breathing and a rapid pulse, they may be going

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: (major allergic reaction)
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: into anaphylactic shock. Seek further medical help immediately. Check to see if the patient is carrying an Epi-Pen or syringe of adrenaline; if so then help them to administer it. Call an ambulance and prop the patient in a sitting position.

sources.title: Hob, kettle, urn
sources.process: The use of a hob, either as a separate unit or as part of a ‘cooker’ powered by gas or electricity. The use of a kettle or urn for heating water.

hazards.label: Burns & scalds
hazards.detail: Flames, hotplates and elements together with hot pans, oven shelves and doors all present a burn hazard. Containers of hot and boiling water also present a scalding hazard.

hazards.label: Fire
hazards.detail: Overheated food or cooking oil and other flammable materials may ignite.

hazards.label: Electric shock
hazards.detail: Any item powered from the electrical mains presents a shock risk if it is damaged.

riskAssessment.label: Burns & scalds
riskAssessment.detail: Sunlight can make flames invisible and some electric hot plates give no indication of being hot. Pans of boiling water are more difficult to control than kettles with a central handle but carrying either a pan or kettle presents a risk of spills. High risk activities include straining water from cooked vegetables, pouring carelessly and reaching over a kettle or pan. The risk of injury is greatest in busy areas with several students working together around one appliance.

riskAssessment.label: Fire
riskAssessment.detail: Oils and fats present the greatest risk of fire in the kitchen.

riskAssessment.label: Electric shock
riskAssessment.detail: A permanently connected item such as a hob presents little risk but a kettle or urn connected via a flexible cable presents a risk if damaged.

controlMeasures: Gas cookers and hobs should, if possible, be installed away from windows, to improve the visibility of flames and reduce the effects of draughts on pilot lights and small flames. The risk of scalding from pans on a hob is controlled by good technique (eg, avoiding overhanging pan handles) which must be taught and by avoiding overcrowding. It is necessary to check that rings above gas burners are firmly in place before starting to use a hob. Care must always be taken with containers of boiling water, avoiding the need to carry them where possible. It is difficult to reduce the risk of fat-pan fires to zero so everyone must be taught how to deal safely with such a fire when it occurs. Open deep fat frying should be avoided. Hair should be tied back and appropriate protective wear should be worn when using the cooker. Frequent visual checks and regular formal inspections reduce the risk of electric shock from faults to a low level. Cleaning methods must not allow water inside the electrical parts. Only kettles with automatic switch off devices should be used.
restrictions: It may be necessary to restrict activities involving hobs unless they are set at an appropriate height for the children using them and fitted with accessible controls.
disposal: For disposal see 3.034.
furtherInformation: Pupils should be taught not to lean across lighted gas burners or hot electric plates. Particular care must be taken with ceramic hobs, which do not show that they are hot, and also after hobs have been turned off, when the rings and plates are no longer visibly hot but have yet to cool down. Care is also required over the positioning of pan handles and guarding against scalds from steam when lifting a saucepan lid. Hair should be tied back and appropriate protective wear should be worn when using the cooker. Dealing with fat-pan fires Although there are special fire extinguishers that are suitable for dealing with burning oil or fat, it is safest to use a fire blanket, damp towel or a tight-fitting lid to cut off the oxygen supply to the fire. This cover must stay in place until the pan is cold to prevent re-ignition. The use of water or the wrong extinguisher can seriously spread the fire with disastrous consequences. Kettles Children need to be taught to think about the risks when handling boiling water. Any kettle chosen for use in food technology should be well balanced when full, have a handle that does not become hot and a lid that cannot fall out when the water is poured. Children must be taught not to remove the lid while the water is being heated, to switch off an electric kettle before pouring and to unplug the lead from the socket before removing it from the kettle. Modern jug kettles are usually safer than types with a central handle on the top but both types can produce a jet of steam at the handle under certain circumstances.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Burns or scalds to the skin
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Cool the affected area under a running cold tap for ten minutes.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Serious burns to the skin
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Send for an ambulance. Cool the affected area under a running cold tap for ten minutes. Watch for difficulty in breathing or faintness. Gently remove jewellery or watches that might be difficult to remove later if the limb swells. Apply a dry dressing held in place by a cotton wool pad secured with a bandage or adhesive tape if the ambulance has not yet arrived.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Electric shock
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Send for a first aider immediately. Taking care for your own safety, break contact by switching off or pulling out the plug. If it is necessary to move the casualty without switching off the supply, use a broom handle or wooden window pole or wear rubber gloves. If the casualty is unconscious and not breathing, check that the airways are clear and begin artificial ventilation. Send for an ambulance. If a trained first aider does not arrive quickly and the casualty has no pulse, consider carrying out cardio-pulmonary resuscitation.

sources.title: Knives
sources.process: Scraping, peeling and cutting vegetables, cutting and trimming meat, filleting and cutting fish, cutting bread.

hazards.label: Cuts
hazards.detail: Fingers and hands may be cut while using knives.

hazards.label: Stabbing
hazards.detail: Stabbing injuries may occur while knives are being carried from the place of storage to the work place or to a sink after use.

hazards.label: Juice in the eye
hazards.detail: Juice may spurt into an eye from fruit while cutting it with a knife.

hazards.label: Infection
hazards.detail: Clean food may become contaminated via the knife or chopping board if it is also used for food that is carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxic products.

riskAssessment.label: Cuts
riskAssessment.detail: The risk is increased when the knife is blunt as greater pressure has to be used to effect the cut and the knife is then more difficult to control. Novices are more likely to cut their fingers than those who have learned appropriate techniques. Risks are greatest in busy areas with students working close together.

riskAssessment.label: Stabbing
riskAssessment.detail: The layout of the workplace can have a major impact on the risks of stabbing. Where knives are carried around the room, the risks are high. Again, risks are greatest in busy areas with students working close together but, with some pupils, there is also a risk of deliberate attacks on each other.

riskAssessment.label: Juice in the eye
riskAssessment.detail: The risk is greatest when cutting fruit such as lemons.

riskAssessment.label: Infection
riskAssessment.detail: The risk of cross-infection is high, particularly if the chopping board is used to prepare food which is to be eaten raw after it has been used for cutting meat.

controlMeasures: Knives should be kept sharp and users must be trained in appropriate techniques. In particular, a chopping board must be used for cutting vegetables. Teaching of the bridge technique for cutting foods will reduce risks. Serrated knives are safer than smooth blades. Knives should be kept centrally, however this increases the risk of accidental cutting and stabbing. Good management and discipline is essential and overcrowding should be avoided if the risk of stabbing is to be controlled. The use of a sawing action to cut fruit is less likely to make the juice spurt than attacking the fruit with a knife point. Although wooden boards are probably safe enough, plastic (eg, polypropylene) boards are preferred for chopping foods because these are easier to sterilise or clean thoroughly and do not harbour bacteria. Separate boards and different knives for meat, fish, vegetables and fruit are a distinct advantage; colour-coded boards are now available.
restrictions: It may be necessary to avoid the use of knives with some classes. While vegetable peelers can be used for some manual tasks, they cannot be used for all. Slicers of the mandolin type (with many parallel blades), which are supplied under varying brand names, are not recommended for use in schools. Food processors may be safer to use than knives. (See 3.016.)
storage: All sharp knives should be stored safely with blades pointing downwards, either in a drawer or a special rack. A ‘shadow board’ or a rack with a space for each rack will assist with checking that all knives have been returned after use.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Juice is in the eyes
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Wash thoroughly for at least ten minutes with water, holding the eyelids apart. Seek medical attention if irritation persists.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Cuts
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: If cuts are minor, ie, of a sort which casualties would normally treat themselves, the wound should be washed clean and a small, sterilised dressing applied.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Severe cuts
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Send for a first aider. Apply pressure on or as close to the cut as possible, using fingers or a pad of cloth. Leave any embedded large bodies and press round them. Lower the casualty to the floor and raise the wound as high as possible. Protect yourself from contamination by blood. Blood splashes or drips should be cleaned up with VirKon as on sheet 3.007.

sources.title: Liquidising, mincing, mixing
sources.process: The use of table-top mixing machines with liquidising and mincing accessories.

hazards.label: Electric shock
hazards.detail: Damage to the casing of the appliance, the plug or to the power cord can present an electric shock hazard.

hazards.label: Injury
hazards.detail: The accessories have sharp cutting blades or screw feeds which may produce injuries if the equipment is misused or if care is not taken during cleaning.

hazards.label: Manual handling
hazards.detail: Some machines are so heavy that they present a manual-handling hazard.

hazards.label: Dust
hazards.detail: Flour dust presents both a health and an allergic reaction hazard.

riskAssessment.label: Electric shock
riskAssessment.detail: Risks may arise from damaged or incorrectly wired plugs, the fitting in the plug of a fuse with an inappropriate rating for the equipment and flexible cables which have been damaged or allowed to become worn, impairing the insulation.

riskAssessment.label: Injury
riskAssessment.detail: Domestic machines are designed so that access to dangerous parts is limited but a small hand could reach the blades of a liquidiser or a long finger could reach the feed screw of a mincer. Any attempt to reach into either accessory while it is on the machine presents a significant risk. Risks are greatest in busy areas with students working close together.

riskAssessment.label: Manual handling
riskAssessment.detail: Lifting a heavy machine from a low cupboard or a high shelf presents a risk of injury to the lower back.

riskAssessment.label: Dust
riskAssessment.detail: Flour dust has now been given a Workplace Exposure Limit (WEL) which means that the concentration of flour in the air must be kept below 30 mg/m3 (15 min ref period)1 and as far below this as reasonably practicable.

controlMeasures: Frequent visual checks and regular formal inspections reduce the risk of electric shock to a low level. (See the General Introduction.) Manufacturers instructions should be followed at all times. Clear instructions for use should be given Users must be trained not to push food down the tube of a mincer with fingers but to use the pushing implement provided and to isolate the machine from the power supply before removing accessories for cleaning. Discipline is essential and overcrowding should be avoided if the risk of injury is to be controlled. Users must be trained to move heavy machines correctly, using two persons if necessary. If any mixer tends to produce a cloud of flour dust, it should either be fitted with a lid or the method of adding flour to the mix should be chosen to minimise the problem.
restrictions: The use of these machines should be restricted to those who are sufficiently mature and competent to follow instructions carefully.
storage: The manual-handling problem can be reduced if storage arrangements are such that heavy machines do not have to be lifted or carried. Blades and attachments should be stored appropriately Cleaning When cleaning knives and attachments, care must be taken over putting the sharp blades into the washing up bowl and removing them from the water, eg, by doing them last. It is advisable to leave blades and attachments to dry in the air after cleaning.
furtherInformation: It is important to ensure that only one student at a time is using the equipment. Particular care should be taken with mixers that have exposed, rotating whisks not to insert spatulas or other tools into the bowl while the mixer is operating: they can become caught and jam the machine. When liquidising hot food, it is advisable to hold a cloth over the top of the liquidiser to ensure that no hot liquid is sprayed at the operator. Many lids will prevent this but some do not do so.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Flour dust is in the eyes
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Wash thoroughly for at least ten minutes with water to prevent scratching of the eye. Seek medical attention if irritation persists.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Cuts
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: If cuts are minor, ie, of a sort which casualties would normally treat themselves, the wound should be washed clean and a small, sterilised dressing applied.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Electric shock
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Send for a first aider immediately. Taking care for your own safety, break contact by switching off or pulling out the plug. If it is necessary to move the casualty without switching off the supply, use a broom handle or wooden window pole or wear rubber gloves. If the casualty is unconscious and not breathing, check that the airways are clear and begin artificial ventilation. Send for an ambulance. If a trained first aider does not arrive quickly and the casualty has no pulse, consider carrying out cardio-pulmonary resuscitation.

sources.title: Microorganisms used in food production
sources.process: Using culinary microbes such as yeast in baking, and bacteria in making yoghurt.

hazards.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
hazards.detail: Eating, or hand to mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxic products may result in gastro-intestinal infection.

riskAssessment.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
riskAssessment.detail: When using culinary microbes, provided that normal practices of hygiene are observed so that all other microorganisms are excluded, there is no significant risk to health. Extensive years of experience indicate that these microorganisms are not hazardous.

controlMeasures: None are needed, other than to ensure that normal hygiene is really observed and that the cultures of microorganisms used are from a reputable source and cannot have become contaminated with other microbes.
disposal: Any unwanted stocks of yeast or yoghurt culture should be mixed with a lot of water and flushed into the foul-water drain.
storage: Dried yeasts may be kept for months but ‘live’ yeasts are best fresh. If they have to be stored, they must be kept cool.
furtherInformation: If other activities involving microbes are contemplated, eg, investigating the growth of bacteria from working surfaces or studying the decay of foods by moulds, there are significant risks since it is not possible to be sure of the type of microorganisms that may be isolated. A normal food technology room in a secondary school or college is, of course, not the place in which such work should be carried out unless the facilities provided are such that potential contamination of food preparation areas is impossible. Instead, arrangements might be made for these investigations to be carried out in the science department. Members of the science department could be consulted, as appropriate, for information on how such investigations should be carried out and how the risks involved in such work should be assessed1. The bacteria in normal yoghurt cultures (that ferment glucose and lactose to lactic acid) are Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus. In the ‘bio’ yoghurts, Bifido bacterium bifidum and Lactobacillus acidophilus are used. Yoghurt drinks (eg, Actimel) use Lactobacillus casei.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Dried yeast is in the eyes
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Wash thoroughly for at least ten minutes with water holding the eyelids open. Seek medical attention if irritation persists.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Poisoning is suspected
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: If a casualty is suffering from nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea with drowsiness or unconsciousness, do not induce vomiting. Provided the casualty is conscious, wash out mouth with water. Obtain medical attention. Reference may be required to the DES publication Microbiology: an HMI Guide for Schools and Further Education (HMSO 1990) ISBN 0112705782 (now out of print), CLEAPSS guidance leaflet PS36, Microorganisns for investigations in schools and colleges, the Association for Science Education publication Topics in Safety (third edition, 2001) ISBN 0863573169 or section 15.2 of the CLEAPSS Laboratory Handbook. The CLEAPSS Laboratory Handbook contains an extensive section that supports teachers and technicians in the practical aspects of using microorganisms, emphasising safe and good practice. (See the information about the COSHH Regulations given in the General Introduction.)

sources.title: Microwaves
sources.process: Heating and reheating food with microwaves in a microwave only oven or one with conventional and steam heating elements as well.

hazards.label: Microwave burns
hazards.detail: If microwaves can escape from the oven, they may be absorbed by human tissue to produce local heating.

hazards.label: Burns and scalds
hazards.detail: Although many food containers used in microwaves do not absorb the waves and do not become hot directly, they will be heated by contact with the hot contents or if the contents boil over.

hazards.label: Superheating
hazards.detail: A liquid may become heated in a microwave to a temperature above its boiling point without boiling (ie, it becomes superheated). When removed and stirred, it can instantly boil over onto a hand holding the container.

hazards.label: Tripping and falling
hazards.detail: The microwave oven is a portable appliance. Trailing leads could cause a tripping accident and the microwave could cause injury if allowed to fall on someone.

riskAssessment.label: Microwave burns
riskAssessment.detail: Ovens using microwaves are designed to minimise this risk by the use of door seals and interlocks that prevent power being applied until the door is properly closed.

riskAssessment.label: Burns and scalds
riskAssessment.detail: There is a real risk of burns or scalds when removing hot food containers from microwave ovens or when lifting lids to stir the contents.

riskAssessment.label: Superheating
riskAssessment.detail: The risk of superheating is difficult to estimate. It depends on the distribution of the item(s) being heated and on the design of the oven. If it happens, the sudden boiling can cause severe scalding.

riskAssessment.label: Tripping and falling
riskAssessment.detail: Although classed as a portable appliance the microwave should be positioned in a permanent and suitable location.

controlMeasures: It is essential for microwave ovens to be regularly maintained and checked according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Instruction should be given on the correct use of individual models of microwave ovens. Although oven gloves are often unnecessary, they should always be used when handling hot food containers in microwave cookers. The risk of superheating may be controlled by putting a small metal spoon in the container used to heat milk or water. The manufacturer’s instructions on this should always be followed. Position microwave where pupils will have ready access without obstructing others, a trolley is useful here. Leads should be kept short.
restrictions: Use only containers made from appropriate materials for heating and cooking in a microwave oven. The following should be avoided: • plastic dairy product containers and other materials made from soft, pliable plastic; • items made from Melamine (it becomes brittle and scorches); • any pottery with a metallic (gilded) rim and all metal containers, including aluminium foil - except in small pieces for shielding; • wooden or wicker containers - except for just warming foods; • coloured paper products.
furtherInformation: Defrosting foods If a microwave oven is used for defrosting food then it is important to observe the manufacturer’s instructions and recommended standing time and check the food regularly. If ice crystals can still be found within the food then thawing should be continued. If the food starts to become warm then it should be allowed to stand for a while to allow the heat to spread or disperse. If the food remains warm then it should be cooked immediately since warm food is the perfect incubator for bacteria. Thawed food must not be refrozen unless cooked thoroughly. The temperature of food cooked in a microwave oven can be tested by using a ‘microwave thermometer probe’, if one is available. This must be cleaned after every use; putting a dirty thermometer into food can add bacteria to it and contaminate it. Use when empty If a microwave cooker is used when empty then there is nothing to absorb the microwaves safely. This may cause components in the cooker to be heated up and produce permanent damage to the system. It is good practice to keep a jug of water in the microwave cooker when it is not in use. Foods with high sugar content Some manufacturers warn against heating foods with a high sugar content with microwaves. Apparently there is a risk that jam or mincemeat may absorb the microwave energy preferentially to produce local heating or even boiling. Testing microwave cookers for leakage Although microwave testers are available, there is not even a recommendation that they should be used to check that any leakage of microwave radiation is negligible.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Burns to the skin
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Cool the affected area under a running cold tap for ten minutes.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Serious burns to the skin
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Send for an ambulance. Cool the affected area under a running cold tap for ten minutes. Watch for difficulty in breathing or faintness. Gently remove jewellery or watches that might be difficult to remove later if the limb swells. Apply a dry dressing held in place by a cotton wool pad secured with a bandage or adhesive tape if the ambulance has not yet arrived.

sources.title: Pest control
sources.process: Pests that may become a problem in food technology rooms and storage areas include rodents: mice and rats; birds: pigeons and sparrows; insects and other arthropods: houseflies, wasps, ants, cockroaches, moths, silverfish, meal and bacon beetles, flour mites and weevils.

hazards.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
hazards.detail: Pests can spread bacterial infections to food during its storage or preparation and gastrointestinal infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxic products. Rodents and flies also carry food-poisoning bacteria in their intestines and can contaminate food by their secretions and droppings.

hazards.label: Poisons on food
hazards.detail: Pesticides can contaminate food and give rise to poisoning which is not an infection. Persons applying pesticides may inadvertently come into contact with the substance directly.

riskAssessment.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
riskAssessment.detail: The risk from pests is low in clean, well-organised premises but if conditions are not clean and pest populations are allowed to build up the risk is increased.

riskAssessment.label: Poisons on food
riskAssessment.detail: The risk that humans may come into contact with the chemicals used in pesticides is low if they are used properly.

controlMeasures: A rigorous policy (see the rules to discourage pest populations below) must be adopted to prevent pest populations building up or becoming a problem. If pests are detected, they must be eradicated using the methods below. In the extermination of pests, positive steps should be taken to avoid exposure. Pesticide formulations available for use in domestic situations are now carefully controlled. They should be obtained only from normal household retail outlets that will only supply approved products carrying a MAFF / HSE number. Unlike other hazardous substances that give only the hazard warning on the label, pesticides give full instructions on the packaging for their safe use. In effect, each pesticide is supplied with its own individual risk assessment which, therefore, must be strictly followed.
restrictions: Most pesticides are unsuitable for use by young persons.
disposal: Surplus solid pesticides may be placed, in their original containers, in the dustbin. Liquids may be diluted and applied to unsurfaced paths or level soil avoiding areas near ponds or other watercourses.
storage: All pesticides must be stored safely and securely away from food.
furtherInformation: Discouraging pests The following rules can be used to discourage pest populations. • Make food storage and preparation areas as inaccessible as possible to pests. • Keep these areas scrupulously clean. • Clear up food spills promptly. • Cover all food during preparation. • Eliminate dark corners and crevices, together with all damp areas. • Ensure all refuse bins are covered. • Use covered metal bins or other metal containers for food storage. • Inspect new deliveries of food for pests. • Watch out for torn bags or holes in cartons. • Be vigilant for signs of droppings, larvae or pupae and dead animals. Eradicating pests If pests become a problem, expert advice can be obtained from the Environmental Health Department of the local authority or from a professional company. Minor pest infestation may be dealt with by pesticides1 from supermarkets provided formulations are chosen carefully, using only those which are recommended for the intended purpose. It is essential to follow the instructions given. Any pesticide formulation that, by its described method of application, may contaminate food should be avoided. Some types of pesticide release their active ingredient more safely as a vapour, while other ‘residual’ formulations are long- lasting and are particularly useful in storage cupboards. Work at home It is sensible to encourage students to adopt similar procedures for pest control in their own homes, to warn of the dangers of pets carrying pests and bacteria into the kitchen or food storage area and to recommend that all pesticides are kept out of the reach of small children.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Exposure to pesticide
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Follow the instructions on the packaging. The use of pesticides is strictly regulated by the Control of Pesticides Regulations 1986. These impose a duty of care to ensure that any pesticide used does not affect the health of any organism other than the pest to be controlled. Employers must ensure that employees are provided with sufficient instruction and guidance so that they may use a pesticide correctly and safely. Pesticides sold for domestic use will have been specially developed for this purpose; they are much less hazardous and will not require protective clothing to be worn. Such pesticides may be used in schools, if appropriate, but it is essential that the instructions provided with the pesticide are followed exactly. (Note that it is now illegal to use in the home or garden any pesticides that have been produced for agricultural or industrial applications.)

sources.title: Portable food processors, mixers & powered tools
