sources.process: The use of hand-held kitchen equipment which comes in several sizes from small battery-powered whisks to machines which really need a stand and table top blenders and smoothie makers

hazards.label: Electric shock
hazards.detail: Damage to the casing of the appliance, the plug or to a mains power cord can present an electric shock hazard. Water inside the appliance can lead to insulation breakdown and to external metal becoming live.

hazards.label: Injury
hazards.detail: Sharp cutting surfaces may be hazardous if the equipment is misused or if care is not taken during cleaning or storage.

hazards.label: Tripping
hazards.detail: Mains leads that trail across the floor present a tripping hazard.

hazards.label: Dust
hazards.detail: Flour dust presents both a health and an allergic reaction hazard.

riskAssessment.label: Electric shock
riskAssessment.detail: Appliances that are repeatedly moved, plugged in and unplugged are liable to damage which increases this risk. If the power cord is long then it can be damaged by trapping in cupboard doors, by being caught in its own mechanism or by touching hot objects on a hob. Holding the whole machine under a tap to wash cutters or beaters can allow water to enter which may present a serious risk.

riskAssessment.label: Injury
riskAssessment.detail: Small grinders, eg, for coffee beans, which often have a top which must be held down to operate the on / off switch, present little risk of injury unless the top is broken and allows a finger to enter. Hand-held mixers have too low a power to cause significant injury with the beaters supplied.

riskAssessment.label: Tripping
riskAssessment.detail: If appliances have to be fitted with long leads that trail across the floor, the tripping risk is significant.

riskAssessment.label: Dust
riskAssessment.detail: Flour dust has now been given a Workplace Exposure Limit (WEL) which means that the concentration of flour in the air must be kept below 30 mg/m3 (15 min ref period)1 and as far below this as reasonably practicable.

controlMeasures: Frequent visual checks and regular formal inspections reduce risks of electric shock resulting from damage to a low level. Users must be taught to remove cutters and beaters (where possible) for cleaning and not to put the whole appliance in the sink or under a tap. The appliance itself and cutters that cannot be removed must be cleaned with a damp cloth or paper while the appliance is unplugged. Users must be trained not to push food down the feed tube of a processor with fingers but to use the pushing implement provided and to isolate the machine from the power supply before removing accessories for cleaning. Clear instructions must be available. If long mains leads cannot be avoided, they must be routed so that there is no risk of anyone tripping over them. If any mixer tends to produce a cloud of flour dust, it should either be fitted with a lid or the method of adding flour to the mix should be chosen to minimise the problem.
restrictions: This type of equipment should be operated by one pupil at a time. Although food processors are very safe to use, some classes may contain pupils who are too disruptive to be trusted with such equipment.
disposal: See 3.034. The Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment Regulations 2006 (the WEEE Regulations) apply.
storage: Any tool that has the potential to be misused should be stored in a secure place.
furtherInformation: When using electric carving knives, it is important to follow guidance from the manufacturer and only use with foods that are suitable for cutting with this equipment. It is also important to ensure that the knife is not connected to the power when inserting or removing the blades. Remember never to wash the blades in water while still attached to the motor. After removal, the blades should be washed with care. The blades are self-sharpening by friction during use and should not be sharpened manually. As with food mixers etc, only one student at a time should attempt to use the equipment.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Flour dust is in the eyes
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Wash thoroughly for at least ten minutes with water to prevent scratching of the eye. Seek medical attention if irritation persists.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Cuts
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: If cuts are minor, ie, of a sort which casualties would normally treat themselves, the wound should be washed clean and a small, sterilised dressing applied.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Electric shock
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Send for a first aider immediately. Taking care for your own safety, break contact by switching off or pulling out the plug. If it is necessary to move the casualty without switching off the supply, use a broom handle or wooden window pole or wear rubber gloves. If the casualty is unconscious and not breathing, check that the airways are clear and begin artificial ventilation. Send for an ambulance. If a trained first aider does not arrive quickly and the casualty has no pulse, consider carrying out cardio-pulmonary resuscitation.

sources.title: Pressure cookers
sources.process: General use of domestic-type pressure cookers.

hazards.label: Explosion
hazards.detail: Failure of a pressure cooker in use, causing the explosive release of its contents.

hazards.label: Overpressure
hazards.detail: The operation of a safety pressure release system can present a hazard from escaping steam and the contents of the cooker.

hazards.label: Burns and Scalds
hazards.detail: Hot surfaces and the sudden release of steam producing scalds.

riskAssessment.label: Explosion
riskAssessment.detail: Pressure cookers have been known to fail (near normal working pressure) at the points where the handles are attached or as a result of fracture of the lid clamps. Both events are rare and the initial cracks probably would not have been discovered by even an expert inspection.

riskAssessment.label: Overpressure
riskAssessment.detail: In use, a pressure cooker should release steam gently. If the outlet becomes blocked by food being cooked or by part of a container, the pressure and temperature rises. A safety device, which is usually a fusible plug, should then operate to release the pressure but, in so doing, the contents boil and may emerge as a scalding jet.

riskAssessment.label: Burns and Scalds
riskAssessment.detail: Failure of the pressure regulating system or of the rubber sealing ring are possible causes of sudden release of steam but the most likely cause is the premature release of the lid or removal of weights before pressure has fallen. The metal surface of the pressure cooker gets hot in use and could cause burns if touched.

controlMeasures: Regular inspection under the regulations (see Further Information overleaf) will limit the risk of explosion. For full guidance see CLEAPSS Guide L214 (parts a to d), Examining Autoclaves, Pressure Cookers and Model Steam Engines. Instruction should be given in the use of pressure cookers. Manufacturer’s instructions should be followed at all times. When using the cooker, constant attention to the sound of escaping steam and/or inspection of the indicator or gauge is required to ensure that the pressure does not become too high. After operation of the pressure release, protection of the hand and arm may be necessary in order to approach the cooker and turn off the supply of heat. The risk of scalds will be reduced if the manufacturer’s instructions (see Restrictions overleaf) are followed carefully when cooling and releasing the lid after use. Oven gloves must be used when handling a hot cooker or the pressure-regulating system. Supervision at this stage is recommended.
restrictions: The cooker must not be opened nor the weights removed when the internal pressure is still high. After cooking is completed, the manufacturer’s instructions on cooling must be followed; usually these require the cooker to cool naturally until an indicator shows that the inside has returned to atmospheric pressure.

Use It is important to ensure that adequate quantities of water have been added, bearing in mind the cooking time. Boiling dry is often the cause of distortion or ‘doming’ of the base which may require the cooker to be failed when the safety inspection is carried out. Manufacturer’s instructions should always be followed.
storage: After use, it is necessary to wash the pressure cooker thoroughly, particularly cleaning the weight support and gasket if soiled with food. With cookers that have a ‘ready-to-serve’ indicator in the safety valve, this must be free-moving and not blocked with food debris. The cooker must be stored completely dry; residual moisture may accelerate pitting of the internal surface.
furtherInformation: Under the requirements of the Pressure Systems Safety Regulations (2000)1, it is necessary for the owners or users of pressure cookers, in their places of work, to make arrangements for a regular inspection of these items against a suitable written scheme of examination. See the CLEAPSS guide L214 parts a to d Examining Autoclaves, Pressure Cookers and Model Steam Engines. An annual safety check will normally be sufficient, unless the items are in very frequent use, eg, every few weeks, in which case it may be appropriate to make a formal examination more often. (Although it is sensible to give pressure cookers at home a safety check, there is no legal requirement that this should happen.) Under the Regulations, the examination of pressure cookers should be conducted by a ‘competent’ person and it is the employer’s responsibility to decide who this should be. Staff in a food technology department may find that their employer has chosen to use the services of an insurance company surveyor to carry out the examinations, often along with the school boilers and equipment in the science department, although there is no requirement that an insurance company is used. The costs of this service may, however, be prohibitive. Employers may, therefore, have chosen to appoint a competent individual to carry out the examinations of equipment in all its establishments, or to authorise an appropriate, competent person in an establishment to carry out the safety checks. It should be noted that the 1999 revision of the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations state that a competent employee is to be preferred.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Burns to the skin
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Cool the affected area under a running cold tap for ten minutes.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Serious burns to the skin
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Send for an ambulance. Cool the affected area under a running cold tap for ten minutes. Watch for difficulty in breathing or faintness. Gently remove jewellery or watches that might be difficult to remove later if the limb swells. Apply a dry dressing held in place by a cotton wool pad secured with a bandage or adhesive tape if the ambulance has not yet arrived. For details of the Regulations and the Approved Code of Practice that gives guidance on their interpretation, see Safety of Pressure Systems, L122, HSE Books, ISBN 071761767X.

sources.title: Purchase and selection of food
sources.process: Choice of supplier and selection of food items.

hazards.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
hazards.detail: Gastrointestinal infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact with, food carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxic products.

hazards.label: Poisons on food
hazards.detail: Poisoning which is not an infection results from eating, or hand-to-mouth contact, with food containing natural toxic chemicals or contaminants from the environment.

hazards.label: Out-of-date foods
hazards.detail: Few food-packaging methods eliminate all microorganisms or enzymes that can change food; they usually slow down the effects.

riskAssessment.label: Food poisoning (Infection)
riskAssessment.detail: If care is not taken in purchasing or selecting food items, there is a possibility that the food may have been contaminated or be carrying pathogenic microorganisms and/or their toxins, resulting in infections when the food is consumed.

riskAssessment.label: Poisons on food
riskAssessment.detail: The risks of food becoming contaminated by transfer from other foods or from a dirty environment are greater in shops without adequate segregation of different food types. Carelessness or ignorance of the appropriate preparation techniques increases the risk of natural toxins being consumed but items presenting risks are restricted to red kidney beans, green or sprouting parts of potatoes and rhubarb leaves.

riskAssessment.label: Out-of-date foods
riskAssessment.detail: Foods that have passed a ‘sell-by date’ or ‘use-by date’ are likely to have a greater risk of infection of the consumer than fresh foods. (See Further Information overleaf for comments on ‘best-before dates’.)

controlMeasures: Fresh foods, including eggs, should be purchased only from reputable shops with good hygiene standards (see Further Information overleaf) and which are popular, so ensuring a rapid turnover of stock. Traces of pesticides or polluting chemicals may remain on fruit and vegetables, which should be segregated in shops and washed off before consumption. Dry red kidney beans must be well cooked to destroy their toxins. Potatoes must be prepared by having green parts and ‘eyes’ removed. Only rhubarb stalks should be cooked and eaten. Packaged foods should always be checked for a future ‘sell-by date’, particularly if they are not to be consumed on the day of purchase.
restrictions: Food in the following situations should be rejected: • unwrapped foods from shelves very close to the floor; • food in damaged, ‘blown’ or rusty tins or containers and vacuum packs with suspect seams; • food that has obviously been mishandled, shows even the slightest evidence of unwanted mould or is past its ‘sell-by date’; • green potatoes or those in a pack size such that they can not be consumed fairly swiftly; • fatty foods such as cheese or pastries that have been wrapped in ‘cling film’. (See 3.019 for more information.)
storage: See 3.017, 3.018, 3.019 & 3.020. If pupils bring in food for food technology work, there should be proper storage arrangements available, both before and after the time for the lesson. The problems of storage of food prior to a lesson can be reduced if the school or college supplies the materials from a central stock.
furtherInformation: Stores with good hygiene standards can be recognised by: • good organisation, eg, loose fruit and vegetables being displayed well away from flowers, fish, meat, dairy and delicatessen items; • being obviously clean (no spills evident in food cabinets or on the floor); • having good lighting; • having hand-washing facilities; • having special facilities for handling raw and cooked foods, ie: separate slicers, boards and small utensils for all different types of foods as well as cooked food products; • proper storage for frozen and chilled foods, ie, with cartons evenly stacked and not above the load line in an open-topped freezer, and by staff handling food: • wearing clean overalls; • having their hair tied back and covered; • wearing minimum jewellery; • having short, clean fingernails with no nail varnish; • being free from coughs, colds and similar infections; • having cuts covered with a food-standard (blue) waterproof dressing; • using tongs or gloves and paper or film to ensure that their hands do not come into direct contact with food. Foods with ‘best-before’ dates ‘Best-before’ dates on food indicate how long the food is expected to be at its best, ie, having a good flavour and texture. After this date, the foods are not necessarily ‘unsafe’ to eat.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Poisoning is suspected
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: If a casualty is suffering from nausea, vomiting or diarrhoea with drowsiness or unconsciousness, do not induce vomiting. Provided the casualty is conscious, wash out mouth with water. Obtain medical attention.

sources.title: Toasting food
sources.process: The use of an electric toaster or a sandwich toaster as a stand-alone, electrically- powered unit.

hazards.label: Electric shock
hazards.detail: An electric toaster has elements which, while not freely exposed, are accessible with a slim metal object such as a table knife and hence present a shock hazard.

hazards.label: Burns
hazards.detail: Flames and elements, together with hot sides and covers, all present a burn hazard.

riskAssessment.label: Electric shock
riskAssessment.detail: The risk of electric shock is greatest when trying to extract a small piece of toast from an electric toaster. Even when the switch is off, an incorrectly-wired appliance can produce a fatal accident.

riskAssessment.label: Burns
riskAssessment.detail: The surfaces of electric sandwich toasters can be very hot. The risk of injury is greatest in busy areas with several students working together around one appliance.

riskAssessment.label: Trips and falling
riskAssessment.detail: The leads on portable appliance can cause dangers of tripping and falling. Sandwich toasters can be heavy and could cause damage to the foot.

controlMeasures: The standard of maintenance on all electrical appliances must be high but this is particularly true of electric toasters and sandwich makers. (See Introduction to Part 3.) Items should be removed from an electric toaster / sandwich makers using a plastic tool, eg, spatula or tongs, designed for high-temperature use. Oven gloves are also advisable. Equipment should be positioned near to socket outlets to prevent leads from trailing. A ‘caution hot sign’ is also advisable.
restrictions: Pupils who are not sufficiently mature should not use electric toasters.
disposal: For disposal see 3.034.
furtherInformation: Sandwich toasters Cleaning an electric sandwich toaster requires care. The plates should be allowed to cool down, the toaster unplugged and then it should be cleaned only with a damp cloth or paper towel; never by immersing it in water.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Electric shock
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Send for a first aider immediately. Taking care for your own safety, break contact by switching off or pulling out the plug. If it is necessary to move the casualty without switching off the supply, use a broom handle or wooden window pole or wear rubber gloves. If the casualty is unconscious and not breathing, check that the airways are clear and begin artificial ventilation. Send for an ambulance. If a trained first aider does not arrive quickly and the casualty has no pulse, consider carrying out cardio-pulmonary resuscitation.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Burns to the skin
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Cool the affected area under a running cold tap for ten minutes.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Serious burns to the skin
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Send for an ambulance. Cool the affected area under a running cold tap for ten minutes. Watch for difficulty in breathing or faintness. Gently remove jewellery or watches that might be difficult to remove later if the limb swells. Apply a dry dressing held in place by a cotton wool pad secured with a bandage or adhesive tape if the ambulance has not yet arrived.

sources.title: Tunnel ovens
sources.process: A tunnel oven cooks food products by passing them through a chamber that is heated. The cooking time is influenced by the speed of the food passing through the oven.

hazards.label: Burns
hazards.detail: Hot surfaces may result in a burn or scald to the skin.

hazards.label: Fire
hazards.detail: Overheated food, fats or cooking oil may ignite.

hazards.label: Entanglement
hazards.detail: Hair, hands and clothing can become entangled in moving parts.

hazards.label: Electric shock
hazards.detail: With any electric equipment there is a danger of electric shock.

riskAssessment.label: Burns
riskAssessment.detail: Handling oven shelves and hot containers often result in minor burns and scalds. The greatest risk occurs when putting items into, and removing them from the oven.

riskAssessment.label: Fire
riskAssessment.detail: Oils and fats present the greatest risk of fire in the kitchen. Build up of debris in oven can cause fires.

riskAssessment.label: Entanglement
riskAssessment.detail: As moving parts are partly exposed, entanglement is possible.

riskAssessment.label: Electric shock
riskAssessment.detail: If properly installed by a qualified electrician then this risk should be minimal. Tunnel ovens should be correctly installed with an appropriate fused switch-disconnector.

controlMeasures: All teachers and pupils need adequate training in the use of tunnel ovens prior to use. Adult supervision is needed at all times. The equipment installed should be of a type where the external casing temperature does not cause burns if touched. Suitable protective equipment should be provided, eg: oven gloves. The oven should be kept clean and free from build up of debris that could cause fires. Long hair, loose clothing should be secured so as not to come into contact with moving parts. Dangling jewellery should be removed.
furtherInformation: Tunnel ovens often require a current supply in excess of 13 amps and will need to be directly connected to a suitable fused switch-disconnector. They should be installed by a qualified electrician and be part of an annual planned maintenance programme as well as regular visual inspections.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Burns or scalds to the skin
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Cool the affected area under a running cold tap for ten minutes.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Serious burns to the skin
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Seek further medical assistance. Send for an ambulance. Cool the affected area under a running cold tap for ten minutes. Watch for difficulty in breathing or faintness. Gently remove jewellery or watches that might be difficult to remove later if the limb swells. Apply a dry dressing held in place by a cotton wool pad secured with a bandage or adhesive tape if the ambulance has not yet arrived.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Fire
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Cover item with damp tea towel. If necessary ring fire alarm and use fire extinguisher.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Entanglement
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Stop the machine with isolator stop switch. Carefully release item caught. Calm pupil.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Electric shock
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Send for a first aider immediately. Taking care for your own safety, break contact by switching off. If necessary move the casualty without switching off the supply, use a broom handle or rubber gloves. If the casualty is unconscious and not breathing, check that the airways are clear and begin artificial ventilation. Send for an ambulance.

sources.title: Waste disposal
sources.process: The disposal of food waste including cooked and uncooked material. Disposal of unwanted / irreparable equipment.

hazards.label: Encouraging pests
hazards.detail: Disposing of waste food unhygienically encourages pests that may then contaminate food.

hazards.label: Injury
hazards.detail: Irreparable equipment from knives to food mixers may constitute a hazard to persons handling waste.

riskAssessment.label: Encouraging pests
riskAssessment.detail: Work in food technology inevitably generates quantities of food wastes that may pose a hazard if pests such as flies, cockroaches or rodents can gain access. These can transfer bacteria to items of food in storage areas or left uncovered during food preparation, causing food poisoning. Handling a dirty refuse bin and dirty lid can spread bacteria to the hands and so onto food, if good personal hygiene is not observed.

riskAssessment.label: Injury
riskAssessment.detail: Any sharp object placed in ordinary refuse can cause injury to cleaners or waste disposal operatives.

controlMeasures: Separate bins should be used for food waste and other wastes. These must be easy to clean and always fitted with a lid that should preferably be foot-operated. Each bin should be lined with a plastic bag of suitable size and a new one used every time the bin is emptied. The bin must be kept clean, especially the lid; the bin should be washed and dried thoroughly every time it is emptied. Hands must be washed thoroughly after touching the inside of the bin or its contents. Sharp, pointed or damaged tools and broken crockery should be placed in a tough container that is sealed before placing it in a dustbin.
restrictions: Much of the electrical equipment in food technology rooms and in other departments comes under the Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment Regulations 2006 (the WEEE Regulations) for disposal. In practice, in most schools the site staff will arrange for the collection and disposal of such equipment. The CLEAPSS guidance leaflet PS 77, The WEEE Regulations, gives further of what is required.
disposal: of unwanted / irreparable equipment. HAZARDS Encouraging pests Disposing of waste food unhygienically encourages pests that may then contaminate food. Injury Irreparable equipment from knives to food mixers may constitute a hazard to persons handling waste.

RISK ASSESSMENT Encouraging pests Work in food technology inevitably generates quantities of food wastes that may pose a hazard if pests such as flies, cockroaches or rodents can gain access. These can transfer bacteria to items of food in storage areas or left uncovered during food preparation, causing food poisoning. Handling a dirty refuse bin and dirty lid can spread bacteria to the hands and so onto food, if good personal hygiene is not observed. Injury Any sharp object placed in ordinary refuse can cause injury to cleaners or waste disposal operatives.

CONTROL MEASURES Separate bins should be used for food waste and other wastes. These must be easy to clean and always fitted with a lid that should preferably be foot-operated. Each bin should be lined with a plastic bag of suitable size and a new one used every time the bin is emptied. The bin must be kept clean, especially the lid; the bin should be washed and dried thoroughly every time it is emptied. Hands must be washed thoroughly after touching the inside of the bin or its contents. Sharp, pointed or damaged tools and broken crockery should be placed in a tough container that is sealed before placing it in a dustbin.

RESTRICTIONS Much of the electrical equipment in food technology rooms and in other departments comes under the Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment Regulations 2006 (the WEEE Regulations) for disposal. In practice, in most schools the site staff will arrange for the collection and disposal of such equipment. The CLEAPSS guidance leaflet PS 77, The WEEE Regulations, gives further of what is required.

Disposal Refuse must not be allowed to accumulate in food rooms and should not be left there overnight. As soon as possible, food waste must be moved to the bin used for kitchen waste, which itself should be covered to exclude pests. Increased use of composting will be encouraged. Irreparable electrical goods will have to go to a recycling centre - many local authorities have schemes now.
furtherInformation: Waste-disposal units Some sinks in food technology may have waste-disposal units fitted. These electrical devices are built into the waste pipe and macerate waste so that it can be flushed away down the foul-water drain. Water authorities do not encourage the fitting of these units now but there is no prohibition on their use. They are designed so that fingers cannot reach the cutters but the handles of teaspoons or other narrow implements can pass through the grill into the macerating region. Clearly, care is needed to avoid damage to either spoons or the unit itself. See CLEAPSS guidance leaflet PS 31, Disposal of Waste in Design & Technology for a summary of the present legal position.

immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Wash thoroughly for at least ten minutes with water to prevent scratching of the eye. Seek medical attention if irritation persists.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Cuts
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: If cuts are minor, ie, of a sort which casualties would normally treat themselves, the wound should be washed clean and a small, sterilised dressing applied. Appendix 3 Food poisoning: The major causes of food poisoning

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Moulds
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Mould fungi cause food spoilage and produce toxic metabolites (mycotoxins including aflotoxin) which are — — harmful when eaten. Aflotoxin has been associated particularly with mouldy cereals and nuts. The presence of mould, which resembles cotton wool, on food is often an indication that the food may be contaminated with other microorganisms. Moulds can develop on any suitable nutrient base providing sufficient moisture, and can grow over a wide range of temperatures. They spread by forming spores, which are released into the air and if they fall on a favourable environment, such as food, germinate and grow to produce a new colony. ‘At risk’ foods include poorly stored dried fruit (figs), bread, beans and nuts but any food may become contaminated.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Parasites in food
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: The only significant risk is from toxoplasmosis; other parasites, such as tapeworms, should not be a problem if — — food is obtained from reputable sources. Infection is most hazardous to those in the ‘at risk’ groups, particularly young children and pregnant women. The parasite can spread to humans in undercooked meat or raw meat and raw vegetables which have been contaminated with infected cat faeces or cat litter. The parasite is found in many animals but can only reproduce successfully in the cat’s gut.

immediateRemedialMeasures.label: Natural toxins
immediateRemedialMeasures.detail: Some food plants contain harmful chemicals, eg, rhubarb and tomato, but the quantities are very small in the — — parts of the plant that are normally eaten. The bean Phaseolus vulgaris, often called the red kidney bean, haricot bean or french bean among other common names, contains a poison which is, however, broken down by heat. Inadequately cooked beans may still be toxic. Solanine builds up in green or sprouting potatoes; if taken in large amounts it leads to gastro-intestinal pain, diarrhoea and could ultimately be fatal. Great care must be exercised if food from the garden or the wild is chosen; particularly guard against mistaken identity when selecting leaves, roots and berries. Certain types of mushroom are poisonous, so care must be taken to use only species known to be safe and accurately identified. Appendix 4 Food Tests: Details of suggested tests
